https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-026-02365-9 Article The apical polar ring is essential during the blood stage of Plasmodium falciparum

Pratima Gurung1,2, Peter S. Back 1,2, Ilzat Ali 1,3, Gabrielle M. Hernandez 1,3 & Jeffrey D. Dvorin 1,2

The apical polar ring (APR) is a defining cytoskeletal structure in apicomplexan parasites, critical for parasite morphology and host cell invasion. However, its molecular composition and function remain elusive in Plasmodium falciparum. Here we identify and characterize PfAPR3 as an APR-resident protein. Conditional knockout of PfAPR3 reveals its essential role in asexual replication. PfAPR3-knockout parasites contact host red blood cells but fail to form a tight junction, resulting in a complete block in invasion. Using PfAPR3 as bait, we identify three additional APR proteins (PfAPR4, PfCHAKRA and PfAPR5) and delineate APR biogenesis with ultrastructure expansion microscopy. Unlike PfAPR3, PfCHAKRA is critical for cytoskeletal network organization. Iterative ultrastructure expansion microscopy further shows PfCHAKRA at the basal APR until mid-schizogony, with PfAPR3 exhibiting dual apical–basal ring localization during schizogony. These findings define the molecular architecture and function of the APR in P. falciparum and have implications for understanding parasite host cell infection.

The apicomplexan parasite Plasmodium falciparum causes the deadliest form of human malaria1, replicating asexually in human red blood cells (RBCs) via schizogony to produce dozens of daughter merozoites per cycle2. Apicomplexan parasites possess a characteristic apical complex3–6, containing the apical polar ring (APR), secretory organelles (rhoptries and micronemes) and, in some apicomplexans, a conoid3,7. The APR is a central component in apicomplexans, identified by electron microscopy >50 years ago3,4,8–12. The apical complex is critical for parasite shape, egress and invasion. In P. falciparum, the APR contains three concentric rings (diameters: 180 nm, 240 nm and 370 nm). The two top rings are connected by a 34-unit bridge structure, while the basal ring is the largest and thickest6. This basal ring is connected to the parasite’s cytoskeleton, known as the inner membrane complex (IMC) and subpellicular microtubules (SPMTs)6,13–15. During schizogony, the IMC forms at the apical end of developing merozoites, later expanding and enveloping them. The APR marks the apex of the IMC and is hypothesized to anchor the SPMTs in apicomplexans4,6,11,12,15–20. Recent studies suggest that the centrosome-associated microtubule organizing center nucleates

microtubules, which are later handed off to the APR10,11,21,22. The APR and its associated cytoskeleton are crucial for parasite shape, cell division and invasion. Despite its prominence in invasive stages6,13,23,24, the molecular components and function of the P. falciparum APR remain incompletely understood. The APR has been extensively studied in Toxoplasma gondii4,6,11,12,17,20,25–28. Only 5 of 11 known T. gondii APR components (APR2/ TGME49_227000, APR3/TGME49_208340, APR4/TGME49_219500, APR5/TGME49_299190 and APR7/TGME49_320030) have Plasmodium orthologues4,12. In Plasmodium berghei, PbAPR1/PBANKA_0907700 and PbAPR2/PBANKA_1334800, orthologues of TgAPR3 and TgAPR7, localize at the apical end of ookinetes4. Recently, PyAPR2 and two associated proteins were localized to the APR in Plasmodium yoelii18. PyAPR2 depletion impairs APR formation and SPMT anchorage, preventing mosquito transmission. However, no APR proteins have been identified in P. falciparum, and the biological function of the APR in human malaria parasites remains unknown. PfAPR3 and its interactors are essential for asexual parasite replication We induced PfAPR3 gene excision with rapamycin and confirmed excision by PCR and western blot (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). PfAPR3-knockout (PfAPR3-KO) parasites showed a 98 ± 0.6% growth reduction in one replication cycle (Fig. 2a). Monitoring egress and invasion every 4 h (44–56 hpi) by Hemacolor staining revealed that PfAPR3-KO parasites showed normal egress but failed to invade new RBCs, remaining adjacent to the RBC surface (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). Collectively, these results show that PfAPR3 is essential for merozoite invasion of RBCs. We tested whether PfAPR3-interacting proteins are essential by inducing knockdown via anhydrotetracycline (ATc) removal. Without ATc, TetR binds target mRNA aptamer arrays, and DOZI sequesters them into stress granules40,41. Without ATc, PfAPR4 levels decreased to 7.8 ± 2.7% of the ATc control, PfCHAKRA to 3.2 ± 0.8% and PfAPR5 to 29.6 ± 11.6% (Extended Data Fig. 2h–j). Replication assays revealed significant growth defects: PfAPR4 (92 ± 3% reduction), PfCHAKRA (98 ± 1% reduction) and PfAPR5 (73 ± 2% reduction) within one cycle (Fig. 2b–d), showing that all three proteins are individually essential.

PfAPR3 is dispensable for IMC formation but modulates SPMT organization U-ExM analysis revealed that IMC formation proceeded normally in PfAPR3-KO parasites. However, unlike wild-type (WT) schizonts that produce individual merozoites, PfAPR3-KO schizonts frequently generated a single multinucleated daughter-cell agglomerate enclosed by IMC, indicating defective segmentation (Extended Data Fig. 4a). To assess SPMT formation and organization, mature parasites were arrested before parasitophorous vacuolar membrane rupture with the protein kinase G inhibitor, ML10 (ref. 42), and stained with ɑ-tubulin. SPMTs formed and anchored to the APR in both WT and PfAPR3-KO parasites. WT parasites showed paired, nearly parallel SPMTs (average angle of 14 ± 1.5° between them), aligned along one side of each merozoite. By contrast, PfAPR3-KO merozoites showed a significantly increased angle between SPMTs (47 ± 2°), with >50% showing disorganized or non-parallel SPMT arrangements (Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). These data show that PfAPR3 is required for proper SPMT alignment. NHS-ester staining confirmed intact apical–basal polarity in PfAPR3-KO parasites, with rhoptries apically positioned, and the basal complex at the basal end (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). The dense APR structure was preserved, indicating that PfAPR3 is dispensable for APR assembly. Thus, PfAPR3 is dispensable for IMC biogenesis, apical polarity and APR formation, but essential for SPMT alignment and merozoite segmentation.

PfAPR3 loss prevents tight junction formation We analysed invasion in synchronized PfAPRDiCre parasites (±rapamycin) after release from ML10-induced arrest, using IFA, live-cell differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy and U-ExM. Merozoite invasion of RBCs proceeds through pre-invasion (attachment and reorientation), internalization (tight junction formation and entry) and ring-stage establishment43–45. During invasion, merozoites induce changes in the RBC cytoskeleton to modulate membrane deformability: pre-invasion causes mild deformation, while internalization induces pronounced, reversible echinocytosis, characterized by a spiky membrane morphology45,46. Time-lapse DIC microscopy revealed that WT merozoites efficiently completed all invasion stages and induced characteristic RBC echinocytosis (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Video 1). Results PfAPR3 is an APR-resident protein in P. falciparum We used rodent malaria APR-resident proteins to identify P. falciparum orthologues4,18,29. We identified PfAPR3 (PF3D7_1141300) as a potential candidate following a BLAST search of the P. falciparum genome30. PfAPR3 shows 44.9% sequence identity with PbAPR1/PBANKA_0907700, which is the orthologue of TgAPR3 (refs. 4,12; Extended Data Fig. 1). To avoid confusion, we named the P. falciparum proteins similar to their T. gondii orthologues throughout. PfAPR3 is ~111 kDa (1,012 amino acids) in size and contains a pleckstrin homology-like domain at residues 876–977. Transposon screens predict that it is essential for asexual replication31,32. To investigate the role of PfAPR3, we generated an inducible knockout strain (referred to as PfAPR3DiCre) in the NF54DiCre(pfs47) background, which expresses split dimerizable Cre recombinase33. We replaced the native PfAPR3 gene locus with a loxP-flanked, codon-altered PfAPR3 tagged at the C-terminus with three copies of the haemagglutinin (HA) epitope (Extended Data Fig. 2a). The strain was verified by PCR, sequencing and western blot (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Immunofluorescence assays (IFAs) revealed that PfAPR3 is undetectable before schizogony, when it appears as a distinct ring-like structure at the apical end of developing and mature merozoites (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 3a). To determine the timing of PfAPR3 expression, we co-stained with PfGAP45, an IMC-associated protein that localizes to the forming IMC in early schizonts (~5 nuclei, 40 h post-invasion (hpi)) and later surrounds mature merozoites34,35. IFA showed that PfAPR3 expression coincides temporally with PfGAP45 and appears at the apex of PfGAP45 in merozoites (Fig. 1a). PfAPR3 localizes apical to PfAMA1, a micronemal marker36. This suggests that PfAPR3 resides at the extreme apical tip of the merozoites, possibly at the APR (Fig. 1b). Ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM) with N-hydroxysuccinimide Alexa Fluor 405 (NHS-ester) staining, which labels the protein-dense APR34,37, showed that PfAPR3 colocalizes with the APR as a discrete ring. The apical ends of SPMTs are positioned beneath both PfAPR3 and the NHS-ester-stained APR (Fig. 1c). These findings establish PfAPR3 as a bona fide resident of the APR in P. falciparum.

PfAPR3-interacting proteins (PfAPR4, PfCHAKRA,PfCHAKRA and PfAPR5) Co-immunoprecipitation using α-HA on late-stage PfAPR3DiCre schizonts followed by mass spectrometry identified 49 high-confidence interactors (≥10-fold enrichment and ≥10 unique peptides across replicates; Supplementary Table 1). We prioritized three uncharacterized candidates—PF3D7_1128900, PF3D7_1138000 and PF3D7_1307900—that are predicted to be essential for parasite replication30,38. PF3D7_1128900 (73.8 kDa) is the orthologue of TgAPR4 (refs. 4,12); thus, we named it PfAPR4. PF3D7_1138000 is a large (335.7 kDa) Plasmodium-specific protein of unknown function. We named it cytoskeletal hook apical key ring-associated protein (PfCHAKRA). PF3D7_1307900 (105 kDa) contains a B-box-type zinc-finger domain39 with 25% identity over this domain to TgAPR5; we named it PfAPR5. We generated dual-transgenic strains (PfGOIiKD) by fusing ten copies of the TetR-binding aptamer and a spaghetti monster V5 (smV5) tag to the 3′ end of each gene in the PfAPR3DiCre background (and PfAPR5 was also tagged with smHA separately in NF54DiCre(pfs47) parasites). These parasites also express TetR-DOZI, a fusion protein between the TetR binding protein and development of zygote inhibited (DOZI). All parasite strains were verified by PCR and western blot (Extended Data Fig. 2d–j). IFAs showed all candidates localized as rings at the merozoite apex, apical to PfGAP45 (Fig. 1d). U-ExM confirmed alignment with the NHS-ester-stained APR (Fig. 1e). Reverse

Because successful invasion requires secretion of micronemes and rhoptries, we tested whether PfAPR3 influences these secretory events. Western blot analysis of culture supernatants detected similar levels of micronemal release of PfEBA175 in WT and PfAPR3-KO (109 ± 24% of WT). By contrast, PfRh2a (rhoptry marker) secretion was significantly reduced in PfAPR3-KO (72 ± 13% of WT) (Fig. 3d). Schizont expression levels were unchanged for both proteins (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h), indicating that PfAPR3 selectively affects rhoptry secretion without altering PfRh2a production. We next examined whether PfAPR3 ablation affects PfAMA1 translocation. PfAMA1 is proteolytically processed and translocated to the merozoite surface during egress, a prerequisite for invasion36,49. IFA on mid- and E64-arrested schizonts revealed normal PfAMA1 expression and merozoite-surface translocation in PfAPR3-KO parasites (Extended Data Fig. 4d), indicating that PfAPR3 does not alter PfAMA1 expression or translocation. Given normal PfAMA1 translocation, we next investigated tight junction (TJ) formation by tracking PfRON4 (a TJ complex component) during invasion44,50,51. In WT parasites, PfRON4 redistributes from the apical rhoptry neck to an arc or ring-like configuration, observed as paired puncta in single z-slices, corresponding to the TJ and then disperses along the parasitophorous vacuolar membrane after invasion. In PfAPR3-KO parasites, PfRON4 remained confined to a single apical focus throughout merozoite attachment and reorientation, with no evidence of TJ formation or characteristic redistribution (Fig. 3e). These results suggest that PfAPR3 is required for TJ formation during invasion. To confirm this, we analysed rhoptry discharge using PfRAP1 (a rhoptry bulb marker52–55). In early invasion, PfRAP1 localized apically

as a small circle in both WT (12 ± 29%) and KO (93 ± 5%) parasites. In mid-invasion, WT and CytoD-arrested controls (12 ± 12%) showed a characteristic C-shaped or doughnut-shaped PfRAP1 pattern, while PfAPR3-KO parasites showed only faint, distorted, doughnut-like patterns (6 ± 1%), indicating limited rhoptry release. They never showed the extensive PfRAP1 spreading along the RBC surface characteristic of R1-peptide-treated parasites54. By late invasion, PfRAP1 localized around the successfully invaded merozoites only in WT parasites (76 ± 24%), confirming failed rhoptry discharge in PfAPR3-KO. Schizont PfRAP1 expression was unchanged, establishing that PfAPR3 selectively impairs rhoptry discharge during invasion (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). U-ExM visualization during invasion stages captured all invasion stages in WT parasites, including rare mid-invasion in WT parasites but only attached and reoriented stages in PfAPR3-KO parasites, with no evidence of internalization (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Collectively, these findings establish that PfAPR3 is essential for post-reorientation invasion by influencing secretion of rhoptry proteins that are required for TJ formation and successful invasion.

PfAPR4 or PfAPR5 deficiency has similar phenotypic consequences as PfAPR3 deficiency To assess the role of PfAPR4 and PfAPR5 during schizogony, we analysed their depletion using U-ExM. PfAPR4- and PfAPR5-deficient parasites showed normal IMC formation and apical polarity but displayed moderate segmentation defects similar to PfAPR3-KO with abnormal multinucleated daughter-cell agglomerates (Extended Data Figs. 2h,j and 6a,c). Some PfAPR5-deficient parasites retained normal morphology, probably reflecting incomplete protein knockdown (30% residual protein) (Extended Data Fig. 2j). PfAPR4-deficient parasites showed disorganized SPMT alignment in >50% of daughter cells, similar to PfAPR3-KO, while PfAPR5-deficient parasites showed less severe SPMT disorganization (Extended Data Fig. 6b,d). On the basis of these similarities to PfAPR3-KO, we infer that PfAPR4 and PfAPR5 are similarly required for invasion but did not perform independent invasion assays.

PfCHAKRA coordinates apical–basal polarity and cytoskeletal organization during schizogony Unlike PfAPR4 and PfAPR5, PfCHAKRA knockdown produced strong morphologic abnormalities in schizonts. In control schizonts, each daughter merozoite was individually enclosed by the IMC (PfGAP45). PfCHAKRA-deficient schizonts showed PfGAP45 enveloping multiple merozoites, forming multinucleated ‘megazoite’ agglomerates, along with occasional PfGAP45 zoids lacking nuclei (Fig. 4a). This segmentation defect was confirmed by transmission electron microscopy (Fig. 4b). PfCHAKRA depletion disrupted apical organelle organization. The APR was largely absent, with only occasional NHS-ester-stained APR (2 or 3 per parasite) remnants visible, probably owing to incomplete knockdown (3 ± 1% residual PfCHAKRA protein; Extended Data Fig. 2i). While control schizonts consistently showed two rhoptries per merozoite associated with the APR, PfCHAKRA-deficient parasites contained single, detached or clustered rhoptries lacking the APR ring or apical positioning (Fig. 4a,b). These findings show that PfCHAKRA is essential for APR formation and rhoptry organization. To examine whether the APR anchors SPMTs, we analysed SPMT organization following PfCHAKRA knockdown. U-ExM revealed excessively long, disorganized microtubules in PfCHAKRA-deficient parasites compared with controls. Notably, these abnormal microtubules were confirmed as SPMTs by polyglutamylated tubulin (α-polyE) staining at their apical ends, distinguishing them from mitotic spindle microtubules13,34,56,57 (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7a). Given that SPMTs nucleate at the centriolar plaque (CP)22,34,56,57, we assessed whether SPMT nucleation is affected by APR loss. To assess whether APR disruption affects apical–basal polarity, we next examined basal complex organization using smMyc-tagged PfCINCH (a basal complex marker58,59; Extended Data Fig. 8). In control schizonts, U-ExM revealed that PfCINCH localized to contracted basal complexes at the centre of ML10-stalled parasites. PfAPR3-interacting proteins show distinct APR localization dependencies Because all four APR proteins are individually essential, we investigated whether they depend on one another for correct localization. We used dual transgenic parasite lines (PfAPR4iKD, PfCHAKRAiKD and PfAPR5iKD), each expressing smV5-tagged PfAPR3-interacting partners, to analyse their colocalization with PfAPR3 (ɑ-HA) under three conditions by U-ExM: (1) both proteins present, (2) partner protein depleted and (3) PfAPR3 knocked out.

PfAPR4–PfAPR3 mutual dependency. U-ExM revealed that PfAPR4 and PfAPR3 colocalized closely (Pearson’s R = 0.70). In PfAPR4-deficient parasites, PfAPR3 staining was spotty or absent by mid-schizonts. Conversely, in PfAPR3-KO parasites, PfAPR4 appeared mislocalized, filling the region enclosed by the basal complex in mid-schizonts (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 9a) before disappearing in late schizonts (Extended Data Fig. 9b). These observations suggest that PfAPR3 stabilizes PfAPR4 at the APR, while PfAPR4 is required for robust PfAPR3 localization at the APR.

PfCHAKRA–PfAPR3 unidirectional dependency. U-ExM showed that PfCHAKRA was basal to PfAPR3 (Pearson’s R = 0.41). In PfCHAKRAdeficient parasites, proto-APRs were mostly undetectable and PfAPR3 staining was largely absent in mid-schizonts, with only occasional PfAPR3-positive APR rings (2 or 3 per schizont), reflecting residual PfCHAKRA in knockdown. By contrast, PfAPR3 depletion did not affect PfCHAKRA localization at proto-APR in mid-schizonts (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Thus, PfCHAKRA localizes to the APR independently of PfAPR3, while APR assembly and PfAPR3 accumulation at the APR are dependent on PfCHAKRA.

PfAPR5–PfAPR3 independence. PfAPR5 showed tight spatial overlap with PfAPR3 (Pearson’s R = 0.89), the highest colocalization among APR proteins. In PfAPR5-deficient parasites, PfAPR3 localized normally. Conversely, PfAPR3 depletion also did not affect PfAPR5 localization (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 9e). Thus, PfAPR5 and PfAPR3 are not dependent on each other for localization, despite their extremely close colocalization. Collectively, these findings reveal that PfCHAKRA acts as the foundational protein, recruiting PfAPR3 to proto-APRs. PfAPR3 and PfAPR4 mutually stabilize each other, while PfAPR5 associates closely with PfAPR3, but neither affects the other’s localization at the APR.

APR biogenesis in P. falciparum While APR assembly in T. gondii proceeds from centrosome-associated arcs to a mature ring structure27, this process is poorly understood in Plasmodium. We tracked PfAPR3 and PfCHAKRA localization during schizogony by U-ExM, in which NHS-ester efficiently labels the protein-dense APR, its precursor (proto-APR) and the CP34. The CP is an unconventional centrosome, forming a bipartite structure with distinct extranuclear and intranuclear regions. The extranuclear region is hypothesized to nucleate SPMTs and is physically connected to the proto-APR34,56. Notably, the CP duplicates once per nuclear cycle but is not readily visible at the end of the schizogony34,60–62. Both PfAPR3 and PfCHAKRA are recruited to the apical end of the extranuclear CP, forming arc-shaped structures that label the NHS-ester-stained proto-APR. Notably, PfCHAKRA is positioned closer to the proto-APR than PfAPR3, suggesting spatial complexity during APR assembly. As the CP duplicates during the nuclear cycle, the proto-APR, along with PfAPR3 and PfCHAKRA, also duplicate, forming paired semi-circles. Maturation into closed APR rings occurred asynchronously; one duplicated CP showed a closed ring-shaped APR, while the other retained an arc-shaped proto-APR. These structures subsequently mature into the closed ring-shaped APRs in the newly formed CPs. At the end of schizogony, when the CP is not visible, the APR ring persisted at the apical end of mature daughter cells, with PfAPR3 remaining associated, whereas PfCHAKRA was no longer visible (Fig. 6a and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Collectively, these results show that APR biogenesis in Plasmodium involves a conserved arc-to-ring maturation, with PfAPR3 and PfCHAKRA occupying distinct spatial positions. While the Plasmodium APR includes three concentric rings6, conventional U-ExM resolved the APR as a single ring. To improve resolution, we applied iterative U-ExM (iU-ExM) with ~15-fold expansion22,63. iU-ExM distinguished two concentric APR rings: a large basal ring and a more apical, dense ring that probably represents the two upper rings merged (Fig. 6b,c and Extended Data Fig. 10b–d). iU-ExM confirmed that PfCHAKRA localizes basal to the PfAPR3 in mid-schizonts (Fig. 6b). Interestingly, PfAPR3 localization differs in mid and late mature schizonts. In late schizonts, PfAPR3 predominantly localized to the largest basal ring (103/103, 100%), whereas in mid-schizonts, it was observed at both basal and apical rings (44/53, 83%). Quantification included 156 APR rings observed from top view across both stages and two biological replicates (Fig. 6c,d).

Discussion In this study, we have identified PfAPR3, PfAPR4, PfCHAKRA and PfAPR5 as essential APR-resident proteins in P. falciparum blood-stage parasites and reveal distinct roles of these components in cytoskeletal organization and host cell invasion. Through live-cell microscopy, we observed that PfAPR3-KO merozoites successfully egress and complete pre-invasion steps but fail to establish a TJ and are unable to invade RBCs. Notably, the RBCs in contact with PfAPR3-KO merozoites showed atypical echinocytosis, characterized by transformation into a rounded sphere with numerous needle-like protrusions. This phenotype closely resembles the effect of R1 treatment, which directly blocks AMA1–RON2 interaction and TJ formation43,64. Taken together, our data suggest that PfAPR3 is required for TJ formation or stabilization, and that its absence phenocopies the effects of direct PfAMA1-RON complex inhibition. Our iU-ExM reveals a spatial and temporal organization of the APR. PfAPR3 localizes to both apical and basal APR rings and physically associates with PfAPR4 and PfAPR5, a complex that persists throughout schizogony. By contrast, PfCHAKRA localizes exclusively to the basal ring during early to mid-schizogony and is absent in late schizonts. The temporal dynamics and distinct functional impacts of these proteins suggest a model in which PfCHAKRA acts as a scaffolding component essential for APR assembly and apical–basal polarization

Methods Plasmid construction and generation of transfected lines PfAPR3DiCre (pPG35). The PfAPR3DiCre parasite strain was generated using a donor plasmid assembled from five PCR-amplified DNA fragments via Golden Gate (GG) assembly with the NEB BsaI-HFv2 kit (E1601L, NEB), following the manufacturer’s protocol. The fragments included the following: (1) the 5′ UTR region, amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with primers oJDD7410/7411; (2) a codon-optimized PfAPR3 gene, amplified from the synthetic gene block GB85 (Biobasic) using oJDD7412/7413; (3) a region containing the linker-3 × HA, LoxP and human dihydrofolate reductase amplified from pPG31 with oJDD7414/7415; (4) the 3′ UTR region, amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with oJDD7416/7417; and (5) the pGEM ampicillin region, amplified from plasmid pPG25 using oJDD7418/7419.

PfAPR4iKD (pPG61). The PfAPR4iKD parasite strain was produced by transfecting the donor plasmid pPG61 into the PfAPR3DiCre parasite. The pPG61 plasmid was assembled from five PCR-amplified fragments using GG assembly. The fragments comprised the following: (1) a 5′ homology region (HR) amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with oJDD8357/8358, and a codon-optimized PfAPR4 gene from gene block GB100 with oJDD8463/8464 (joined by PCR sewing); (2) smV5, amplified from pPG03 with oJDD8331/8332; (3) TetR-DOZI and blasticidin S deaminase (BSD) cassette, amplified from pPB69 with primers oJDD8333/8334; (4) a 3′ HR region amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with oJDD8361/8362; and (5) the pGEM backbone, amplified from pPG25 with oJDD8337/8338.

PfCHAKRAiKD (pPG72). The PfCHAKRAiKD parasite strain was generated by integrating the pPG72 construct into the PfAPR3DiCre parasite background. The pPG72 plasmid was assembled from five PCR-amplified fragments using a GG reaction. Piece 1 was obtained by PCR sewing a 5′ HR region from 3D7 genomic DNA (oJDD8375/8376) with a codon-optimized region from gene block GB102 (oJDD8466/8378); piece 2 was smV5, amplified from pPG03 with oJDD8331/8332; piece 3 comprised TetR-DOZI and BSD cassette, amplified from pPB69 with primers oJDD8333/8334; piece 4 was 3′ HR from 3D7 genome with oJDD8379/8380; and piece 5 was the pGEM backbone, amplified from pPG25 with oJDD8337/8338.

PfAPR5HA (pIA39). The pIA39 was generated by assembling four PCR-amplified DNA fragments using GG assembly. The fragments included the following: (1) a 5′ HR region amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with oJDD8875/8876; (2) smHA and BSD, amplified from pPB69 with oJDD8877/8878; (3) a 3′ HR region amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with primers oJDD8879/8880; and (4) the pGEM backbone, amplified from pPB69 with oJDD8818/8881. The assembled construct was used for transfection to generate the PfAPR5HA parasite in PfNF54DiCre background.

PfAPR5iKD (pIA74). The PfAPR5iKD parasite strain was produced by transfecting the donor plasmid pIA74 into the PfAPR3DiCre parasite. The pIA74 plasmid was assembled with BsaI GG assembly. The fragments comprised the following: (1) an APR5 cassette from pIA39 with oJDD8879/9640 and (2) an smV5, TetR-DOZI, BSD and pGEM cassette, amplified from pPG72 with primers oJDD9639/8878.

PfCINCHMyc (pPB168 in PfCHAKRAiKD). The PfCINCHMyc parasite strain was generated by transfecting the donor plasmid pPB168 into the PfCHAKRAiKD parasites. For pPB168, GG assembly of two fragments was used. Piece 1 was amplified from pPB85 using oJDD9415/9435 and contained the pGEM backbone with 5′ and 3′ HRs; piece 2 was amplified

from pPB136 using oJDD9436/9418 and contained smMyc and a yUra1 selection cassette. All CRISPR–Cas9 guide plasmids were generated by annealing and ligating oligonucleotides corresponding to guide sequences into the BpiI-digested pRR216 plasmid. The pRR216 plasmid contains SpCas9 and a U6 promoter-driven guide RNA cassette58. For PfAPR3DiCre parasites, plasmid pPG36 with guide oligos oJDD7420 and oJDD7421 was used. For PfAPR4iKD parasites, guide plasmids pPG62 (oJDD8403/8404), pPG63 (oJDD8405/8406) and pPG64 (oJDD8407/8408) were used. For PfCHAKRAiKD parasites, guide plasmids pPG73 (oJDD8419/8420) and pPG74 (oJDD8421/8422) were used. For PfAPR5HA parasites, pIA44 (oJDD8578/8579) and pIA45 (oJDD8580/8581) were used as guide plasmids. For PfAPR5iKD parasites, guide plasmids pIA44 (oJDD8578/8579) and pIA45 (oJDD8580/8581) were used. For PfCINCHMyc parasites, pPB04 (oJDD7514/7515) was used as a guide plasmid.

Parasite culture and maintenance The P. falciparum NF54DiCre(pfs47) laboratory strain, obtained from M. Treeck33, was used as the parental background for transfections and controls. Parasites were cultured in RPMI-1640 (Sigma, R6504) with 25 mM HEPES (4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid; EMD Biosciences), 0.21% sodium bicarbonate (VWR, 0511), 50 mg l−1 hypoxanthine (Sigma) and 0.5% Albumax II (Invitrogen) using human O+ erythrocytes (Valley Biomedical). Cultures were maintained at 37 °C under a gas mixture of 5% CO2, 1% O2 and 95% N2. Tightly synchronized ring-stage parasites were obtained by subjecting late-stage schizonts to a 60% Percoll (GE Healthcare), followed by sorbitol lysis at 0–4 hpi (refs. 65,66).

Transgenic parasite generation To generate transgenic parasite strains (PfAPR3DiCre, PfAPR4iKD, PfCHAKRAiKD, PfAPR5HA, PfAPR5iKD and PfCINCHMyc), 25 μg of linearized donor plasmid DNA and 25 μg of SpCas9-gRNA plasmid were co-transfected into Percoll-purified late schizonts (either NF54DiCre(pfs47) or PfAPR3DiCre or PfCHAKRAiKD background) using a P3 Primary cell 4D-Nucleofector X Kit L (Lonza, V4XP-3024) and an Amaxa 4D electroporator (Lonza, programme FP158). Post-electroporation, parasites were transferred to 4% haematocrit (HCT) fresh RBCs in complete RPMI and cultured as above. Drug selection was initiated 5 h later: 2.5 nM WR99210 (Jacobus Pharmaceuticals) for all strains; plus 0.5 μM ATc (10009542, Cayman Chemicals) and 2.5 μg ml−1 blasticidin (B12150-0.1, Research Products International) for iKD parasites; plus 150 nM AD1 (OSSK_722448, Princeton Biomolecular Research) for PfCINCHMyc. Parasite clones were isolated by limiting dilution in 96-well plates, expanded and verified by PCR using gene-specific primers (Supplementary Table 2) and whole-genome sequencing (PfAPR3DiCre; SeqCenter; aligned with Geneious Prime 2024). For rapamycin-induced excision of target genes, 0–4-hpi ring-stage parasites were treated with 100 nM rapamycin for up to 12 h at 37 °C. Followed by three RPMI washes and return to culture67. For ATc removal, Percoll-purified schizonts were washed thrice and resuspended ±ATc.

Reagents and antibodies PCRs used the PrimeSTAR GXL DNA Polymerase kit (Takeda, R050A) per manufacturer’s protocol, except elongation at 60 °C. Oligonucleotide (Life Technologies) and gene block (IDT or Biobasic) sequences are available in Supplementary Table 2. A comprehensive list of all antibodies (concentrations, host species and suppliers) are provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Replication assay Synchronized PfAPR3DiCre parasites (DMSO or 100 nM rapamycin) were diluted to 0.25% parasitaemia and 1% haematocrit. Parasite growth was monitored over two consecutive intraerythrocytic cycles. At days 0, 2 and 4, 100 μl of culture was collected, washed with 0.5% (w/v) BSA in PBS and stained with SYBR green nucleic acid stain (1:1,000; Invitrogen S7563; 20 min at room temperature in the dark). Samples were washed and resuspended in 1 × PBS. Infected RBCs were quantified using a BD FACSCalibur with CellQuest Pro (BD Biosciences, 100,000 events per sample). Data were processed in FlowJo X and GraphPad Prism 9. Results represent the mean ± standard deviation (s.d.) of three independent biological replicates.

Attachment assay The attachment assay was performed48 with slight modifications. PfAPR3DiCre parasites were synchronized by Percoll-sorbitol (2-h window) ± DMSO or rapamycin. Parasites were stalled with 25 nM ML10 (BEI Resources) for 2 h pre-egress. Percoll-purified schizonts were counted using a haemocytometer (Hausser Scientific Levy/Dark-Line counting chamber, 3500) and plated at 0.5 ml per well in 24-well plates at 2% parasitaemia with 2% HCT ± 2 μM cytochalasin D (Millipore Sigma, C8273). After 3 h of invasion, samples were quantified by flow cytometry (as above). Heparin at 50 U ml−1 and 25 nM ML10-stalled parasites served as controls. Three independent biological replicates were performed. Attachment efficiency was calculated for each replicate by normalizing to the mean attachment rate of DMSO (%) and gating per Extended Data Fig. 5.

Western blot analysis Synchronized late-stage schizonts were saponin-lysed (0.02% w/v in PBS + SigmaFast protease inhibitor cocktail; Sigma-Aldrich). Parasite pellets were PBS-washed and boiled in 1× Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad) with BME at 95 °C for 5 min. Proteins (1 × 108 parasites per lane) were resolved on 4–20% Tris–glycine–SDS gel (Bio-Rad; 120 V). Proteins were transferred overnight (30 V, 4 °C) to a nitrocellulose membrane (Bio-Rad) using a wet transfer system. Membranes were blocked with LI-COR Odyssey blocking buffer for 1 h at RT, probed with primary and IRDye-conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 3). Blots were imaged on a LI-COR Odyssey CLx imaging system and quantified using LI-COR Image Studio 4.0 (volume measurement tool). Uncropped blots are provided in source data.

To measure secretion of invasion ligands (PfEBA-175 and PfRh2a) in culture supernatant. Percoll–sorbitol-synchronized parasites (0–3-h interval) were treated ± DMSO and rapamycin. After RBC rupture, culture supernatants were clarified (1,400 rpm, 4 min, then 6,000 rpm, 5 min), mixed with 2× Laemmli sample buffer, resolved by SDS–PAGE and analysed by western blot as above.

IFA For slide-based IFA, thin blood smears were air-dried and fixed with 4% (v/v) paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS for 10 min at RT, followed by three 1× PBS wash. Fixed smears were permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min at RT, then washed three times with 1× PBS for 3 min each. Samples were then BSA-blocked (3% w/v in PBS; 1 h RT) and stained with primary antibody (overnight at 4 °C; diluted in 0.5% BSA in PBS; Supplementary Table 3). After a PBS wash (3 × 5 min), secondary antibodies (1:1,000 in 0.5% BSA in PBS) and, where appropriate, wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) for RBC membrane staining were applied for 45 min of incubation at RT in the dark. Slides were PBS-washed (3 × 5 min), followed by Hoechst 33342 (1:5,000; 20 min at RT in the

dark), PBS-rinsed and mounted with Vectashield Vibrance Antifade mounting media (Vector Laboratories, H-1700). For standard coverslip IFAs, parasites were settled onto poly-D-lysine-coated coverslips placed in 24-well plates at 37 °C for 20 min, then processed as described for slide-based IFA.

Image acquisition Z-stacked images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope equipped with Airyscan 2 and a ×63 oil immersion objective. Images were processed by Airyscan processing or joint deconvolution using Zen software and analysed with FIJI72.

U-ExM U-ExM was performed73. Briefly, synchronized parasites were settled on poly-D-lysine-coated coverslips in 24-well plates for 20 min at 37 °C. Parasites were PFA-fixed (4% v/v PBS, 37 °C, 20 min), three times PBS-washed and cross-linked overnight (37 °C; 1.4% v/v formaldehyde + 2% w/v acrylamide in PBS). The next day, gels polymerized in monomer solution (19% sodium acrylate, 10% AA, 0.1% N,N′-methylenebisacrylamide in 10× PBS), TEMED and ammonium persulfate in a pre-chilled gelation chamber (5 min ice; 1 h 37 °C). After polymerization, coverslips and gels were transferred to a 6-well dish containing 1 ml denaturation buffer (200 mM SDS, 200 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris, pH 9) for 15 min with gentle agitation to detach the gels. The detached gel was then incubated with 1.5 ml denaturation buffer in a microcentrifuge tube at 95 °C for 90 min to achieve complete denaturation. Gels were expanded by incubating in 25 ml deionized water (ddH2O) for 30 min at RT (repeated thrice). Gels were PBS-washed (2 × 15 min) and blocked with 3% BSA in PBS for 30 min at RT. Small pieces of gel were cut and incubated with the respective primary antibodies (3% BSA in PBS; overnight at 4 °C). The following day, the gels were washed thrice with 0.5% Tween-20 in PBS for 10 min each and then incubated with secondary antibodies, NHS-ester (for general protein staining) and SYTOX (for nucleic acid staining) for 2.5 h in the dark. The gels were then washed with 0.5% Tween-20 in PBS for 10 min and re-expanded (ddH2O; 30 min). Expanded gels were placed on a poly-D-lysine-coated imaging dish and imaged using a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope with Airyscan 2 and ×40 or ×63 objectives. Images were processed in Zen software and analysed with FIJI72. For colocalization analysis between PfAPR3 and its interacting partners, we manually defined a region of interest (ROI) on fluorescence images using FIJI72 to restrict analysis to the APR region. For each ROI, colocalization between the two channels (PfAPR3 and its interacting partners) was assessed using the Coloc2 plugin. Pearson’s correlation coefficient was calculated to quantify the degree of colocalization with Costes’ automatic thresholding used to minimize background contribution and ensure unbiased analysis. To quantify the angle between two SPMTs in individual schizonts, we used the SNT option of the Neuroanatomy plugin in FIJI for manual tracing74. For each selected pair of SPMTs, the first and last coordinates (x, y and z) of each SPMT were recorded to define their direction vectors. Assuming that the SPMTs were straight lines in three-dimensional space, the angle between the two SPMTs was calculated using the following formula:

cos θ =

⃗A. ⃗B

| ⃗A|| ⃗B|

where ⃗A and ⃗B are the direction vectors of the two SPMTs. To minimize bias, file names were randomized so that SPMT tracing and measurements were performed in a manner blinded to the experimental condition. Only pairs of SPMTs that were clearly visible and fully traceable throughout their length in each daughter cell were included in the analysis. The analysis was conducted across three independent biological replicates, with three schizonts examined per replicate. In each

iU-ExM For iU-ExM22,63,75, PfAPR3DiCre schizonts were Percoll-purified (60%), settled on poly-D-lysine-coated coverslips and fixed with 4% PFA in PBS as U-ExM. The first anchoring step was performed overnight. Monomer solution I (with DHEBA) was added to fill the gelation chamber, followed by incubation on ice (15 min) and polymerization (37 °C, 45 min). Gels were denatured (85 °C, 90 min in buffer) and expanded overnight in water (~5-fold expansion). After expansion, gels were PBS-washed, blocked in 3% BSA, stained with primary and secondary antibodies, and re-expanded with water. For iteration, gels (1.5 cm2) were washed thrice with activated neutral gel and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Gels were subjected to a second round of anchoring solution (37 °C, overnight). The following day, gels were washed in monomer solution III (with BIS) and incubated (37 °C, 1 h). Gels were then washed with 200 mM NaOH (1 h RT), PBS washed until the pH reached 7 and finally expanded overnight in water (~15-fold expansion factor). For imaging, gels were secured (superglue) on poly-D-lysine dishes and imaged with a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope with Airyscan 2 and a ×63 objective. Images were processed using Zen’s Airy-processing software and analysed with FIJI72.

DIC live-cell microscopy For DIC live-cell imaging, 0–2 h synchronized PfAPR3DiCre parasites (5% parasitaemia, 1% HCT) were treated ± 100 nM rapamycin. Percoll-purified schizonts were ML10-arrested (25 nM, BEI Resources) for 2 h before egress. Parasites were washed twice with pre-warmed RPMI, mixed with fresh RBCs and settled in a 35-mm glass-bottom imaging dish (CellView, 627871). Imaging used a Zeiss LSM 980 microscope (DIC prism, ×63 oil) in a pre-warmed microscope chamber. Parasites were imaged every 2.5 s for 30 min. A minimum of three independent biological replicates were performed.

Affinity-based immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry Synchronized PfAPR3DiCre and PfNF54DiCre schizonts (300 ml each, at 3% parasitaemia, 2% HCT; 40–48 hpi) were saponin-released (0.05% saponin in PBS + SigmaFast Protease Inhibitor Cocktail, Sigma). The parasite pellets obtained were resuspended in 1 ml of RIPA lysis buffer (50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate and 0.1% SDS) supplemented with protease inhibitors and incubated for 1 h at RT on a rotator. Lysates were then sonicated using a microtip sonicator (20% amplitude, 2 × 30 s on ice, 1 min interval). To remove haemozoin and insoluble debris, lysates were centrifuged (maximum speed, 30 min; 4 °C; Eppendorf 5428). Supernatants were incubated with α-HA (Pierce 88836; overnight 4 °C rotation). After incubation, beads were washed thrice with RIPA in PBS. The beads were subsequently resuspended in 50 μl of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and analysed using LC–MS/MS (Taplin Mass Spectrometry core facility at Harvard) on a Thermo Orbitrap mass spectrometer using the data-dependent acquisition mode. Summed intensities for each protein obtained in both sample and control parasites were compared, and proteins with ≥10 unique peptides (n = 2 replicates) were considered for further analysis.

Statistics and reproducibility For all imaging experiments, including slide-based IFA, standard IFA, U-ExM and live-cell imaging, as well as western blot analyses, a minimum of three independent biological replicates were performed to ensure reproducibility. Immunoprecipitation experiments were conducted with two biological replicates. Replication assays were conducted with three independent biological replicates, with each biological replicate including three technical replicates. Results from

all biological replicates, each consisting of technical triplicates, were pooled and presented together in single graphs for analysis. For quantification of schizont and ring-stage parasitaemia by air-dried thin smears, a minimum of 10 random fields was counted per sample, totalling 1,000 cells analysed across 3 independent biological replicates. The angles between two SPMTs were measured in three independent biological replicates. For each biological replicate, 3 schizonts per condition were analysed, with a minimum of 20 pairs of SPMTs per schizont evaluated. Statistical analyses for all experiments were performed using GraphPad Prism software.

# Article

# Essential nucleus-apical pole linkage maintains division ﬁdelity during Plasmodium progeny formation

Buyuan He 1,6, Ilzat Ali 2,3,6, Lilian P Dorner 1, Monami Roy Chowdhury1, Yvonne Sokolowski-Adams1, Evgeniya Abadzhieva1, Arne Reich1, Marilena Wittmaack 1, Julia M Sattler 1,4, Friedrich Frischknecht 1,4 & Jeffrey D Dvorin 3,5

# Abstract

Plasmodium parasites, the causative agents of malaria, undergo complex replication within vertebrate and insect hosts, presenting unique opportunities for therapeutic intervention. A key challenge during these replication events, i.e., schizogony in vertebrate red blood cells and sporogony in oocysts within mosquitos, is ensuring the faithful partitioning of nuclei and organelles into the numerous daughter cells that form at once from a single parental cell. While nuclear microtubule-organizing centers, or centriolar plaques (CPs), have been hypothesized to play a central role in this process, the molecular mediators linking CPs and organelles remain incompletely deﬁned. Here, we characterize the roles of two striated ﬁber assemblin (SFA) homologs, SFA1 and SFA2, in replication of Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium berghei across two hosts. We show that these SFAs form a physical bridge between the CP and the nascent apical poles of daughter cells, facilitating high- ﬁdelity progeny formation during schizogony and sporogony. Loss of SFA function disrupts merozoite and sporozoite formation, with profound consequences for transmission. These ﬁndings identify striated ﬁber assemblins as essential organizers of parasite morphogenesis and potential targets for anti-malarial therapies.

Subject Categories Cell Adhesion, Polarity & Cytoskeleton; Cell Cycle; Microbiology, Virology & Host Pathogen Interaction https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-026-00836-7 Received 19 August 2025; Revised 27 May 2026; Accepted 5 June 2026 Published online: 3 July 226

## Introduction

Malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes and caused by the eukaryotic parasites of the genus Plasmodium, which belongs to the phylum Apicomplexa that also includes other disease-causing parasites such as Toxoplasma and Cryptosporidium. Plasmodium parasites infect a

range of species-speciﬁc vertebrate hosts. Plasmodium falciparum is the deadliest species of human malaria parasites, while Plasmodium berghei infects rodents. Decades of malaria research and public health efforts have led to a substantial decrease in the global burden of the illness as well as improvements in treatment options. However, the emergence of P. falciparum resistance to all available antimalarials and insecticide resistance in mosquitoes have slowed progress toward eradication, signifying a need for the discovery of novel targets for a new generation of antimalarial therapeutics and preventives (Alonso and Noor, 2017; Greenwood et al, 2008; World Health Organization, 2024). The parasite life cycle is complex, encompassing replicative stages inside the intermediate vertebrate host and the deﬁnitive insect host (e.g., Anopheles mosquitoes for P. falciparum and P. berghei). These stages occur in drastically different environments, imposing challenges on the parasite to maintain ﬁdelity in its cellular functions while undergoing morphological changes to adapt to external conditions. Due to these selective pressures, the parasite has evolved essential cellular processes divergent from their host cells that serve as attractive targets for next-generation therapy development. Therefore, improving our understanding of fundamental Plasmodium biology across the various life cycle stages can help address current challenges in malaria eradication. The parasite’s unique modes of replication inside the different hosts represent such divergent processes—the asexual blood stage in the vertebrate host and oocyst development in mosquitoes—both generating many morphologically distinct, haploid daughter cells from a single parent cell (Cowman et al, 2016; Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gubbels et al, 2020). Thus, studying the mediators of replication across these distinct hosts provides a holistic view of how the parasite survives and proliferates. Schizogony is the mode of asexual replication inside the vertebrate red blood cells (RBCs) during which daughter cells known as merozoites form inside a single parent cell. To do this, the parasite replicates its DNA and undergoes karyokinesis multiple times without cytokinesis, followed by a single semisynchronous cytokinetic event known as segmentation to generate dozens of merozoites at once (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gerald et al, 2011; Gubbels et al, 2020; Rudlaff et al, 2020). Plasmodium oocyst development at the mosquito midgut wall forms transmissible, haploid daughter cells, or sporozoites, via an analogous asexual replication process known as sporogony (Gubbels et al, 2020; Sinden and Strong, 1978). The parent cell, called an oocyst, completes multiple rounds of endopolygeny-like events, i.e., DNA replication without karyokinesis, while partitioning into putatively distinct islands of cytoplasm known as “sporoblasts.” As individual nuclei are partitioned off, a massive cytokinetic event forms thousands of sporozoites (Araki et al, 2020). These sporozoites subsequently move to the mosquito salivary glands for transmission to a new vertebrate host. Central to Plasmodium’s ability to form many daughter cells in a complex, single round of cytokinesis is the maintenance of cell division ﬁdelity. Successful production of invasive daughter cells requires the inheritance of one nucleus per daughter cell, in addition to a complete set of organelles, including a mitochondrion, an apicoplast, an endoplasmic reticulum, a Golgi apparatus, and the components of the apical complex (Elaagip et al, 2022; Rudlaff et al, 2020; Struck et al, 2005; van Dooren et al, 2005; Verhoef et al, 2021). Interactions or close associations between the different compartments have been shown to occur in Plasmodium and related parasites and might be important for cellularization (Guttery et al, 2020; Oliveira Souza et al, 2022; Vaishnava and Striepen, 2006; Verhoef et al, 2024). In schizonts, the ﬁnal round of karyokinesis and organelle segregation coincides with the cytokinetic event in which the membrane-associated cytoskeletal components of each forming merozoite, the inner membrane complex (IMC) and basal complex, envelop one complete set of organelles (Rudlaff et al, 2020). During oocyst development, massive cytokinesis occurs by a cytoskeleton-assisted budding-like process, with the nucleus and each set of other organelles entering the budding membranes to form sporozoites (Araki et al, 2020). This high-ﬁdelity cellular division in the setting of a complex parent cell with multiple nuclei and multiple copies of each organelle suggests a strict coordination between nuclear division, organellar replication and inheritance, and daughter cell formation. However, the molecular mediators of this coordination are incompletely understood in Plasmodium, representing a major knowledge gap. A physical connection between the nucleus and the budding daughter cell has been established in Toxoplasma gondii. This parasite replicates asexually in the host cell via endodyogeny, a process during which a single parent cell divides into two complete daughter cells. During budding, a ﬁber composed of striated ﬁber assemblin (SFA) homologs links the nuclear envelope-associated microtubule-organizing center (MTOC), or centrosome, and the apical end of dividing daughter cells (Francia et al, 2012). SFA proteins were ﬁrst identiﬁed in the green algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Goodenough and Weiss, 1978; Lechtreck et al, 2002; Lechtreck, 2003; Ringo, 1967; Weber et al, 1993). They are the main components of the root microtubule-associated striated ﬁbers of algal ﬂagella. Interestingly, the asexual forms of Plasmodium and Toxoplasma lack a ﬂagellum, but, in the case of T. gondii, an SFA ﬁber still forms. This ﬁber emerges from the centrosome and terminates inside the apical conoid structure of the forming daughter cell (Engelberg et al, 2025; Francia et al, 2012). Parasites lacking TgSFAs fail to initiate budding, resulting in multinucleated parent cells without discernable daughter cell structures. This observation underscores the importance of SFAs in coordinating cell division. T. gondii and Plasmodium diverged ~540–800 million years ago and have evolved distinct features (Douzery et al, 2004).

Hence, studying the SFAs in Plasmodium across both its bloodstage and mosquito-stage development can illuminate foundational similarities and reveal key variations in how the parasite orchestrates division in different cellular environments. Plasmodium schizogony is also coordinated by the MTOC of each nucleus through spindle dynamics that drive closed mitosis (Francia and Striepen, 2014). The dividing nucleus is closely associated with the forming apical ends of daughter merozoites (Liffner et al, 2023). As the nucleus duplicates and divides, the associated forming apical end also divides. The MTOC is part of the centriolar plaque (CP), a multiprotein complex that includes both nuclear and cytoplasmic components (Moore and Sinden, 1974; Tomasina et al, 2021). The nuclear portion of the CP, or inner-CP, initiates the intranuclear microtubules (Arnot et al, 2011; Bertiaux et al, 2021; Liffner et al, 2023; Simon et al, 2021). It consists of centromeric and kinetochore proteins that coordinate karyokinesis, such as nuclear division cycle 80 protein, PfNuf2, and PfCENH3 (Hoeijmakers et al, 2012; Li et al, 2024a; Volz et al, 2010), in addition to a putative spindle pole body protein that likely bridges the nuclear and cytoplasmic portions of the CP (Machado et al, 2023). A few components of the cytoplasmic portion, or outer-CP, have also been reported, including the centrins (Mahajan et al, 2008; Simon et al, 2021; Voß et al, 2023), an Aurora-related kinase (Reininger et al, 2011), and an Sﬁ1-like protein (Wenz et al, 2023). They appear to contribute to intranuclear microtubule dynamics during schizogony; however, the full function of the outer- CP, including its putative connection to the forming apical pole, is yet to be elucidated. The role of the CP during oocyst development inside the mosquito host is also poorly understood. A rootlet ﬁber connecting the CP with the apical end of budding sporozoites had been visualized by electron microscopy since the 1970s (Schrevel et al, 2008; Sinden and Strong, 1978), but its composition remained unknown. Here, we characterize the two SFA orthologs, PfSFA1/PbSFA1 and PfSFA2/PbSFA2, in P. falciparum during schizogony and P. berghei during sexual stage and oocyst development. Using microscopy, genetics, and biochemical techniques, we establish the critical function of PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 to connect the CP of each nucleus with a nascent apical end inside a schizont, ensuring that the ﬁdelity of merozoite formation is maintained. Furthermore, we identify two additional proteins that interact with PfSFA2, PF3D7_0703600 and PF3D7_1339700, that may also contribute to the apical-nuclear connection. In P. berghei, we ﬁnd that the SFAs make up the rootlet ﬁber during sporozoite formation within oocysts in the mosquito host. Loss of either PbSFA1 or PbSFA2 leads to profound defects during sporozoite budding and a complete lack of salivary gland sporozoites, establishing an essential role for these proteins in the mosquito host and for transmission. These ﬁndings establish SFAs as the critical bridge between the CP and the forming apical pole across two distinct Plasmodium replicative stages and hosts.

## Results

PfSFA2 and likely PfSFA1 connect the centriolar plaque and the forming daughter cell during asexual replication in human RBCs

To determine whether Plasmodium SFAs play a role in daughter cell formation during replication, we ﬁrst compared the SFA homologs across Plasmodium, Toxoplasma gondii, and Chlamydomonas

We identiﬁed two SFA homologs, SFA1 (PF3D7_0803200/ PfSFA1 or PBANKA_1227000/PbSFA1) and SFA2 (PF3D7_1432900/ PfSFA2 or PBANKA_1012000/PbSFA2) in P. falciparum and P. berghei (Fig. 1A; Appendix Fig. S1A). Plasmodium SFA2 is similar in size to SFA proteins in other species, consisting of a short N-terminal head domain and a rod domain that has the characteristic repeat regions of the SFA family predicted to form an α-helical structure by AlphaFold (Jumper et al, 2021; Lechtreck, 2003; Varadi et al, 2023). PfSFA2 and PbSFA2 are largely similar in their amino acid sequence, sharing 66% amino acid identity (Appendix Fig. S1B). Plasmodium SFA1 proteins also contain an α-helical rod domain of similar size to SFA2, but are unique in that they are ~2.5 times the size of a canonical SFA due to a large unstructured head domain. While the C-terminal rod domain regions of PfSFA1 and PbSFA1 are highly conserved, the low conservation in the head domain leads to an overall identity of ~48% (Appendix Fig. S1B). PfSFA1 shares a 30% amino acid identity with TgSFA1 and 40% with TgSFA3, while PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 only share a 25% identity with each other (Appendix Fig. S1B). Similarly, PfSFA2 and TgSFA2 share a slightly higher amino acid identity than PfSFA2 does with PfSFA1. These ﬁndings suggest that Plasmodium SFA1 is more closely related to TgSFA1 and TgSFA3 than to Plasmodium SFA2 and TgSFA2, and that the common ancestor of SFA1 and SFA2 predates the divergence of these species. Our ﬁndings were further corroborated in a recent comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of SFA paralogs (Heiss et al, 2025). To determine the localization of the SFAs in Plasmodium asexual blood stage, we endogenously labeled PfSFA1 or PfSFA2 with a high-avidity spaghetti monster-V5 (smV5) epitope tag (Viswanathan et al, 2015) and visualized them by immunoﬂuorescence assay (IFA) using Airyscan super-resolution microscopy (Figs. 1B and EV1A). The multicopy number of epitopes within the smV5 tag allowed for higher signal and better signal-to-noise ratio compared to lower copy-number epitopes (such as 2xV5), which produced a dimmer ﬂuorescence signal, making it too difﬁcult to robustly pinpoint localization. In schizonts, both PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 localized to a punctate structure near the outer-centriolar plaque (CP), identiﬁed with antibodies against centrins (Liffner et al, 2023; Mahajan et al, 2008). The PfSFA2 signal was observed as soon as the centrin signal appeared at each nucleus, duplicated along with centrin, and appeared the brightest when the inner membrane complex (IMC, anti-PfGAP45 (Jones et al, 2006)) began to expand, signaling the onset of segmentation (Fig. EV1A). Then, it disappeared by the end of segmentation. To decipher more precisely the localization of PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 in schizonts, we performed ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM) on three distinct schizogony stages (Fig. 1C). A ﬂuorescent dye conjugated to NHS ester (NHS ester for short) that nonspeciﬁcally stains protein-dense structures allows for visualization of mitotic spindles, CPs, and forming apical ends throughout schizogony (Bertiaux et al, 2021; Liffner et al, 2023). In early schizonts, the duplicated outer-CPs, observed by centrin staining, localized above the intranuclear mitotic spindles and below the protein-dense regions where structural components of daughter cells are forming apical to the nucleus (Fig. 1C, top panel). PfSFA2 localized between each centrin and the forming apical end consistently during asynchronous nuclear divisions. Next, in midschizonts, when the parasite began the ﬁnal round of mitosis, the apical poles duplicated one last time and separated (Fig. 1C, middle

panel). The ﬁrst rhoptry anlage of a pair, the dense globular organelles that house parasite invasion proteins, forms beneath the nascent apical polar ring (APR) (Anaguano et al, 2024; Cowman and Crabb, 2006). At this stage, PfSFA2 continued to bridge the outer-CP and the forming apical region of the daughter cells. Finally, during segmentation, when the basal complex (BC) ring became visible, an elongated PfSFA2 structure was observed between the outer-CP and the fully formed APR, although the PfSFA2-containing structure was not clearly visible by NHS ester alone (Fig. 1C, bottom panel). With U-ExM, PfSFA1-smV5 signal also localized between the outer-CP and the apical pole (Fig. EV1B). However, the localization appeared less robust compared to PfSFA2-smV5. This is likely due to the modiﬁcation of the PfSFA1 C-terminus with a large epitope tag like smV5 interfering with its function. The parasites seemed to fare better with a smaller epitope like 2xMyc (Fig. 2; Appendix Fig. S2A); however, we were unable to visualize the SFAs clearly with this tag. Nonetheless, the presence of a signal between the outer-CP and the apical pole suggests a similar localization pattern between PfSFA1 and PfSFA2, and the difﬁculty in modifying the PfSFA1 C-terminus implies the importance of this protein region in its function.

PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 are important for blood-stage replication and likely belong to a single structure

TgSFA2 and TgSFA3 are essential for endodyogeny (Francia et al, 2012). To test the importance of PfSFAs in blood-stage schizogony, we generated ﬂoxed parasite strains with the endogenous PfSFA1 or PfSFA2 ﬂanked by loxP sequences in a parental parasite that expressed a rapamycin-dimerizable split Cre (DiCre) recombinase (Collins et al, 2013a; Knuepfer et al, 2017; Tiburcio et al, 2019). Given the initial difﬁculty producing the PfSFA1 inducible knockout (iKO) strain, we attempted the modiﬁcation in multiple DiCre-expressing parental strains. Ultimately, the modiﬁcation was successfully achieved in 3D7(pfs47)DiCre strain (Knuepfer et al, 2017), generating the PfSFA1loxP iKO strain. The PfSFA2 inducible knockout parasite (PfSFA2loxP iKO) was generated in the NF54(pfs47) DiCre(CG6)attB strain (Fierro et al, 2023) (Appendix Fig. S2B,C). Both transgenic strains were conﬁrmed for genomic integration by PCR (Appendix Fig. S2D). Upon rapamycin treatment to KO either PfSFA1 or PfSFA2, there was a marked growth defect compared to parasites treated with the negative control (DMSO) (Fig. 2A; Appendix Fig. S2A). To quantify the defect, we used the ratio of the parasite multiplication rates (PMR), deﬁned as the PMR of the KO parasite divided by the PMR of the DMSO control. A higher PMR ratio corresponds to a more ﬁt parasite with a less severe growth defect. We observed a PMR ratio of 56 ± 1% for PfSFA1 iKO parasites and a ratio of 65 ± 4% for PfSFA2-iKO parasites, suggesting a comparable defect between the two lines. We do not attribute this partial growth defect to an incomplete KO since a complete rapamycin-induced excision of the modiﬁed locus was observed for each strain by PCR (Appendix Fig. S2D). Moreover, an absence of PfSFA2-smV5 signal after KO was conﬁrmed by IFA for the PfSFA2loxP iKO strain (Appendix Fig. S2E). Instead, this incomplete defect could be due to a partial rescue by other proteins. PfSFA2 is important for maintaining the ﬁdelity of bloodstage replication

At the end of segmentation, fully formed daughter merozoites were visible by U-ExM, wherein each merozoite was bound by a plasma membrane, containing an APR at its apical end, and a BC at the basal end, all visible by the NHS ester-conjugated dye (Fig. 3A,B; Movie EV1) (Liffner et al, 2023; Morano et al, 2023). In a normal merozoite, a pair of equally sized dense rhoptries were observed protruding from the APR, and 1–3 subpellicular microtubules (SPMTs, yellow) ran along the spine of the merozoite from the APR toward the basal end. Each merozoite also inherited a single mitochondrion (stained by MitoTracker, magenta). Lastly, each daughter merozoite contains exactly one nucleus (blue) necessary for the continuation of the life cycle. To characterize the function of PfSFAs during asexual replication, we arrested parasites at the end of segmentation with a small molecular inhibitor of Protein Kinase G, either Compound-1 (Collins et al, 2013b) or ML10 (Baker et al, 2017), in PfSFA2-present (DMSO) and PfSFA2-absent (Rapa) conditions to visualize morphological defects in merozoite formation. In PfSFA2-absent schizonts, multiple nuclei are found in the residual body, a membrane-bound compartment containing leftover schizont materials after segmentation (Liffner et al, 2023; Rudlaff et al, 2020), whereas all nuclei are packaged into merozoites in a 1:1 ratio in control parasites (Fig. 3A; Movies EV1 and 2). Concurrently, we observed merozoites surrounded by plasma membrane without nuclei in PfSFA2-absent schizonts, suggesting a disruption in the linkage between the nuclei and the forming merozoites (Fig. 3B). We quantiﬁed the number of nucleated (#Nuc = 1) and anucleate (#Nuc = 0) merozoites per schizont in both conditions across three biologically independent experiments and found that nearly all merozoites contained a single nucleus when PfSFA2 was present whereas on average 32 ± 1% of the merozoites lacked a nucleus upon PfSFA2 KO (Fig. 3C).

In addition to the defect in nuclear inheritance, we also observed that the number of rhoptries per APR was highly variable in PfSFA2-absent parasites (Fig. 3B,C). On average, 29 ± 2% of the APRs were associated with more than two rhoptries, while 7 ± 1% of the APRs only had a single rhoptry. Moreover, the sizes of the rhoptries associated with the same APR could vary; some APRs contained rhoptries of relatively similar size, while others were associated with rhoptries of drastically different sizes. Occasionally, we observed detached rhoptries inside merozoites or the residual body, and merozoites with two APRs (Fig. EV2B). Notably, the rhoptry abnormalities were observed in both nucleated and anucleate merozoites, although anucleate merozoites tended to display more pronounced abnormalities in rhoptry size and number. These ﬁndings suggest that PfSFAs are also important for maintaining ﬁdelity of rhoptry pair formation. However, it is unclear whether this is a direct function of the SFAs or a function of other structures proximal to the SFAs, such as the CP. Another notable defect upon PfSFA2 KO was a higher variance in SPMT count per APR. In control parasites, APRs were associated with a single SPMT in 9 ± 2% of APRs. However, when PfSFA2 was absent, 32 ± 2% of APRs are associated with a single SPMT, and 4 ± 1% of APRs had no discernable SPMT signal (Fig. EV2D). We also performed all prior analyses with the double iKO strain and found a similar pattern of morphological defects, with these parasites having a slightly higher variance in phenotype compared to the single iKO parasites, marked by a higher spread of the data points (Fig. EV2C,D). Qualitative analysis of Compound-1-stalled PfSFA1-KO schizonts also revealed similar phenotypes as PfSFA2- KO schizonts, including congregation of nuclei and abnormally formed rhoptries inside residual bodies and anucleate merozoite formation (Fig. EV2A). It is worth noting that the DMSO-treated PfSFA1 iKO and double iKO parasites also exhibited morphological defects to a small degree (Fig. EV2), further demonstrating the hypomorphic nature of these strains, likely caused by epitopetagging at PfSFA1 C-terminus. Nonetheless, the similarity in morphological defects observed between PfSFA2 single iKO and PfSFA1/PfSFA2 double iKO parasites quantitatively and between PfSFA1 single iKO and the other iKO parasites qualitatively further demonstrates that the absence of a single SFA homolog is sufﬁcient to disrupt ﬁber function. During schizogony, vital organelles like the mitochondrion and the apicoplast also expand, divide, and partition into individual merozoites (Rudlaff et al, 2020; Verhoef et al, 2024). Given the centrosome-centered hypothesis of apicomplexan parasite cell division (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gubbels et al, 2020), the presence of anucleate merozoites in PfSFA2 KO parasites presented an opportunity to interrogate the importance of the nucleus (and the CP) for the inheritance of these organelles. We found that 86% of all anucleate merozoites still contained a mitochondrion (Fig. 3B). We also observed apicoplast presence in anucleate merozoites by IFA (Fig. 3D). These ﬁndings show that nuclear inheritance is not required for the successful inheritance of mitochondrion and apicoplast into merozoites, suggesting that the partitioning and/or maintenance of these organelles likely require other factors. Overall, we show that SFAs are important for maintaining the connection between each nucleus and the forming apical pole during blood-stage schizogony. They also seem to play a role in the formation and/or stability of structures at the apical region, including the rhoptries and SPMTs.

Discovery of novel proteins between the centriolar plaque and the apical pole

Given the partial growth defect observed in schizonts deﬁcient in SFAs, we hypothesized that there may exist other components of the rootlet ﬁber. To identify these proteins inside the crowded space between each pair of the CP and apical pole, we performed a coimmunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiment using PfSFA2-smV5 as bait and a cytoplasmic protein PfEIF3H-smV5 as a control to capture stable interactors of the rootlet ﬁber. We selected two proteins of unknown function as potential interactors of PfSFA2, PF3D7_0703600 and PF3D7_1339700/ PfPEARL (Protein Enriched at the Apical-Rootlet Linkage), from a list of co-IP hits (Dataset EV1) for further characterization. PF3D7_0703600 is a 34 kDa protein containing a β-giardin-like domain (Lechtreck, 2003), while PfPEARL is a 231 kDa protein with no predicted domains. By endogenously tagging each with an epitope in the PfSFA2-smV5 strain (genomic integration veriﬁed by PCR in Appendix Fig. S2I), we found both to be closely associated with PfSFA2 (Fig. 4A). We then used U-ExM to reveal in detail that PF3D7_0703600 localized between PfSFA2 and the protein-dense structure of the inner-CP, similar to the localization of centrin but with a clear overlap with the PfSFA2 signal (Fig. 4B). Given the close evolutionary relationship between Alveolata SFAs and Fornicata β-giardins (Heiss et al, 2025), these data suggest that PF3D7_0703600 may play a role in connecting the outer-CP with the SFA rootlet ﬁber. We performed further characterization of PfPEARL. In earlier schizonts, U-ExM showed clustered PfPEARL puncta that partially overlapped with PfSFA2 but also localize more apically (Fig. 4C, left panel). In later schizonts, when the APR separated from the CP during the ﬁnal round of nuclear replication, PfPEARL primarily localized to the more apical position (Fig. 4C, right panel). In this later stage of schizogony, PfPEARL colocalized with the apical tip of the SFA ﬁber present within the interior region of the APR. Interestingly, PfPEARL became undetectable prior to the disappearance of PfSFA2 (Fig. EV3). To determine the importance of PfPEARL in blood-stage replication, we inserted the 10xTet aptamer after the endogenous C-terminus. These parasites were engineered to also express the

PbSFA1 and PbSFA2 form long ﬁbers connecting the centriolar plaque and the apical polar ring during oocyst development

Next, we aimed at investigating the role of SFAs during oocyst development and sporozoite formation. To examine if the SFAs are part of the rootlet ﬁber during sporozoite formation (Schrevel et al, 2008; Spreng et al, 2019), we used Plasmodium berghei to characterize PbSFA1 and PbSFA2 by C-terminal tagging with GFP, followed by confocal microscopy. We ﬁrst generated the transgenic parasite lines PbSFA1-GFP and PbSFA2-GFP to localize the proteins individually (Appendix Fig. S3). We were unable to detect GFP signals by live-cell imaging in murine RBCs, likely due to the low expression levels of PbSFAs as evidenced by the need of a high-avidity epitope tag to visualize PfSFAs. Nonetheless, the SFA signals were readily detected during sporozoite formation in oocysts (Fig. 5A,D). Non-synchronized oocysts were imaged at 12–15 days post infection to investigate all steps of sporozoite budding using spinning disc confocal microscopy. Typically, sporozoites are formed over three distinct phases: initiation, intermediate, and elongation. During the initiation phase, the nuclei containing several CPs align below the plasma membrane of the sporoblast, and the IMC is formed beneath the membrane as the membrane generates subtle buds above the nuclei (Araki et al, 2020). The nuclei are oriented with the CP facing the plasma membrane, and the rootlet ﬁber begins to emerge from the CP and connects to the central part of the bud (Schrevel et al, 2008). In the intermediate phase,

the buds begin to elongate and the nuclei separate, with one CP remaining per nucleus, which at this point is still located in the sporoblast cytoplasm. During this phase, a long and electron-dense rootlet ﬁber becomes prominently visible in transmission electron microscopy (Schrevel et al, 2008; Spreng et al, 2019). Finally, in the elongation phase, each nucleus is packaged into individual elongating buds, followed by a mitochondrion. In oocysts not yet undergoing sporogony, the GFP signal was absent, but during the initiation phase of sporozoite formation, short punctate signals could be detected emanating from the nuclei (Fig. 5A,D ″initiation″ phase). With advancing sporogony, the GFP signals became longer, reaching over 3 μm in length during the elongation phase of sporogony. The Hoechst signals were also elongated at this phase, suggesting that the nuclei were already pulled into the buds (Fig. 5A,D, ″elongation″ phase). On average, the PbSFA1-GFP signal in the elongation phase was 1.6 ± 0.7 μm in length while the PbSFA2-GFP signal was 2.2 ± 0.5 μm in length with aspect ratios of around 5 and 7, respectively (Fig. 5B,E). Once sporozoites were fully formed, the PbSFA1-GFP and PbSFA2-GFP signals disappeared and could not be detected after sporozoite entry into the salivary glands (Fig. 5C,F). These ﬁndings suggest that the two SFAs are part of the rootlet ﬁber that elongates during sporozoite budding and disassembles once sporozoites have formed.

PbSFA KO inhibits sporozoite budding

To investigate the morphological differences of budding sporozoites between the PbSFA-KO mutants and wildtype, we used transmission electron microscopy to analyze chemically ﬁxed and thin-sectioned midguts 12, 15, and 18 days post infection (Fig. 7A,B). Initially, sporozoite buds formed at the plasma membrane in the vicinity of the nuclei (Sterling et al, 1973). In both WT and mutant lines, we found the buds delimited by the inner membrane complex that appeared as a thickened membrane (Fig. 7C,D). In WT parasites, we regularly found a rhoptry anlage in the early buds between the nascent apical end and the nucleus (Fig. 7C). We also found part of the rootlet ﬁber that connected the CP of the nucleus to the nascent apical end (Schrevel et al, 2008; Spreng et al, 2019) (Fig. 7C). The average length of the rootlet ﬁber was 0.4 ± 0.2 μm at initial budding stage and 1.2 ± 0.4 μm at elongated budding stage, similar to the data from the ﬂuorescence images of the PbSFA1- GFP and PbSFA2-GFP lines. In the mutants, however, rhoptry anlagen were rarely observed and remained in the sporoblast instead of localizing within the budding tip. We also failed to detect any rootlet ﬁber during early budding (Fig. 7D,E). The nuclei, however, were initially positioned below the plasma membrane in mutants just as in wildtype. Intriguingly, some nuclei in the mutants appeared even closer to the nascent apical end, possibly due to the lack of the rhoptry anlage (Fig. 7D). The nucleus is pulled in as sporozoites elongate during budding (Schrevel et al, 2008; Spreng et al, 2019) (Fig. 7C). Yet, in longer protrusions of the mutants we did not ﬁnd any nucleus. Instead, the nuclei of the mutants remained in the sporoblast (Fig. 7F). Also, rhoptries were rarely observed in the elongated buds of mutant parasites and did not appear at the tip of the buds unlike in wildtype. Instead, they often appeared at the rear in conjunction with the mitochondrion or accumulated in the sporoblast (Figs. 7F and EV4B,D). Intriguingly, these rhoptries were electron-dense and elongated, suggesting that they can mature without proper positioning. Mitochondria were found in some elongated buds of the mutants (Figs. 7F and EV4D), which in WT parasites were only packaged into the budding sporozoites once the nucleus was pulled in (Vanderberg and Rhodin 1967). This suggests that mitochondrial packaging might be independent of nuclear packaging, similar to our observations of the PfSFA mutants in the blood stage. The

apicoplast is found near the nucleus in sporozoites (Kudryashev et al, 2010). While we also found apicoplasts in close vicinity of the nuclei inside the buds of budding WT sporozoites (Fig. EV4C), we did not ﬁnd apicoplasts in the buds of mutants. Instead, some apicoplasts were found near nuclei that remained in the sporoblast of the mutants (Fig. EV5E,F), contrary to our observations of the PfSFA mutants in the blood stage. Strikingly, we observed that in parasites lacking either of the PbSFAs, the IMC was not limited to the forming bud but spread across the plasma membrane of the sporoblast, indicating a stark dysfunction in sporozoite formation (Figs. 7F and EV4D,F). The close proximity of mitochondria to the IMC in these mutants might suggest that the transportation and packaging of mitochondria mainly rely on the connection with the IMC, which had also been demonstrated in T. gondii (Oliveira Souza et al, 2022). Together, these data suggest a massive disruption of organelle packaging during sporozoite formation.

3D tomography reveals perturbed inter-organellar relationships in PbSFA mutants

To investigate the previous observations in more detail, we obtained serial sections from chemically ﬁxed infected midguts, generated tomograms from the individual sections, and joined these tomograms into larger volumes (Beyeler et al, 2024; Spreng et al, 2019). In these 3D reconstructions, we could visualize the entire SFA rootlet ﬁber in WT parasites as previously reported (Spreng et al, 2019) (Figs. 8A,B and EV5A–C; Movies EV3 and 4). Interestingly, they also allowed us to visualize an electron-dense spot at the edge of the rhoptry anlagen facing the rootlet ﬁber, indicating a possible connection between the two that may ensure the proper positioning of the rhoptries (Figs. 8A and EV5A and Movie EV3). This density could only be observed in rhoptry anlagen when rootlet ﬁbers were present, suggesting a possible linking function between organelle and ﬁber. Taken together, these 3D data expand on and support the ﬁndings from single sections in mutants lacking either of the PbSFAs, which showed elongated and electron-dense rhoptries in the sporoblast but not in the bud (Figs. 7F and EV4B). We also found elongated rootlet ﬁbers in the WT sporozoites with the nucleus partly pulled into the bud (Figs. 8B and EV5B; Movie EV4). The rootlet ﬁber also appeared in close association with the apicoplast (Fig. EV5B; Movie EV4), but to reveal a possible connection would require further investigation using cryogenic ﬁxation to better preserve the structures. In both elongated sporozoite buds, the mitochondrion was positioned behind the nucleus. The 3D reconstructions of the mutants yielded eight initiating and one elongated budding events for PbSFA1-KO, and seven initiating and two elongated budding events for PbSFA2-KO (Fig. 8C–F; Movies EV5–8). These conﬁrmed the absence of the rootlet ﬁber and the rhoptry anlage as observed in the 2D data (Fig. 7D). The data in mutants also revealed that the apicoplast was located near the nucleus in the sporoblast and the mitochondrion was positioned near the bud (Fig. EV5E,F). Intriguingly, the tip of the buds appeared in a different shape in the mutants than in the wildtype (Fig. EV5C–E). In WT budding events, the tips were almost ﬂat, likely due to the formation of the APR, while some of the tips of mutant buds were more dome-shaped, suggesting a possible APR mis-assembly.
