## Discussion

High-ﬁdelity cell division is a fundamental requirement for all living organisms to ensure accurate transmission of genetic material and proper segregation of cellular components. In model eukaryotes such as yeast and mammalian cells, tightly regulated mitotic checkpoints and cytoskeletal dynamics ensure that chromosomes are duplicated and partitioned evenly, while

organelles are distributed to daughter cells with precision (Gibieža and Petrikaitė, 2021; Jongsma et al, 2015; Kixmoeller et al, 2020; Meraldi et al, 2004). Many fundamental processes required for division are universally conserved, while specialized functions have evolved across different domains of life (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Li, 2013; Sunchu and Cabernard, 2020; Vleugel et al, 2012). The protozoan apicomplexan parasites exhibit highly divergent and often unconventional modes of replication, such as endodyogeny, endopolygeny, schizogony, and binary ﬁssion (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gubbels et al, 2020). These modes differ not only in the number of progenies produced per division cycle but also in how nuclei, organelles, and cytoskeletal components are coordinated and partitioned. Despite this diversity, these modes require a high degree of regulation to ensure ﬁdelity, especially given the parasites’ reliance on accurate nuclear and organelle inheritance for infectivity and survival. In Plasmodium, the asexual blood-stage replication cycle and oocyst development represent key points where such ﬁdelity is vital. Using P. falciparum and P. berghei for asexual blood-stage and sexual developmental characterization, respectively, we show here that a rootlet ﬁber made of SFA1 and SFA2 proteins plays a critical role in maintaining this ﬁdelity. An analogous ﬁber in developing Toxoplasma tachyzoites originates from the centrosome, which has long been hypothesized to be an important mediator of all apicomplexan cell division (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gubbels et al, 2020). The centrosome-equivalent structure in Plasmodium, the CP, functions similarly to other apicomplexan centrosomes, but its unique features, such as a lack of distinct centrioles and other components that make up the T. gondii centrosome, indicate a mechanistic divergence (Mahajan et al, 2008; Tomasina et al, 2021). During replication, the CP is intimately associated with the nucleus and anchors the mitotic spindle, thereby inﬂuencing the accurate segregation of chromosomes. Beyond this function, emerging evidence, including this study, suggests that the cytoplasmic portion of the CP (or the outer-CP) also contributes to the organization and formation of daughter cells through interactions with SFA-based rootlet ﬁbers that extend toward the apical ends of forming daughters (Engelberg et al, 2025; Francia et al, 2012). In schizogony and sporogony, these rootlet ﬁbers form between the CP and the forming apical end, becoming more pronounced during sporogony as they elongate with budding, and disappearing before daughter cell formation is complete. Our observation of anucleate merozoites and sporozoites in SFA-depleted parasites shows that if the outer-CP is no longer connected to the apical end, then the organelles are no longer properly organized in the progeny. Intriguingly, SFAs are not required for nuclear replication, as WT and SFA-KO P. berghei schizonts form comparable numbers of

nuclei. While the SFAs are important for efﬁcient nuclear inheritance, in the absence of SFAs, nucleated merozoites capable of invading RBCs still form. In contrast, infectious P. berghei sporozoites failed to form in the absence of either PbSFA1 or PbSFA2 (Fig. 8). Although rare sporozoite-like structures were observed, they lacked nuclei. This difference in nuclear inheritance could have resulted from functional redundancy of nearby structures or components in merozoites. A more likely reason may lie in the intrinsic difference between segmentation during schizogony and budding during sporogony that allows the much smaller merozoites to envelope some of the nuclei by chance due to spatial proximity or crowding, while the nucleus requires tethering to the much longer sporozoite via the rootlet ﬁber to get inside the bud. Thus, the packaging of nuclei into sporozoites may be a more active process than its counterpart in schizogony. We also observed defects in structures associated with the APR, namely the rhoptries and SPMTs. This raises a fundamental question of the apical attachment site of the rootlet ﬁber. While we were unable to discern the exact location of the apical tip of the ﬁber by expansion or electron microscopy, we always localized the tip of the PfSFA2 signal at the space inside the merozoite APR. Similar localization of the rootlet ﬁbers could also be found in sporozoites by electron tomography. Currently, there is little knowledge of the structures in this region besides the apical docking site of the rhoptries (Martinez et al, 2022). The presence of the SFAs near this region suggests that rhoptry biogenesis and proper positioning may be dependent on the rootlet ﬁber or the proximity to the outer-CP. In fact, we observed an electron density potentially linking the rhoptry anlagen in budding sporozoites to the rootlet ﬁber, suggesting that these structures are likely part of a larger complex. Prior studies have demonstrated that rhoptry positioning and maturation are highly ordered processes, thus disruption of the elements coordinating this could contribute to lower merozoite infectivity and failed sporozoite formation (Anaguano et al, 2024; Bannister et al, 2000; Liffner et al, 2021). Intriguingly, rhoptries were rarely found in the elongating sporozoite buds lacking SFAs, but they appeared to be anchored normally, though in varying numbers, in merozoites, suggesting another curious difference between the two stages that awaits molecular explanation. In T. gondii, γ-tubulin, the microtubule nucleation factor, has been localized to the conoid of nascent daughter buds (Engelberg et al, 2025; Haase et al, 2024). However, whether this localization contributes to both intraconoidal MT (ICMT) and SPMT formation, or ICMT alone, is unknown. Since Plasmodium species do not have a distinct conoid-like structure or ICMTs, the nucleation site of cytoplasmic tubulin-based structures, such as the SPMT, remains contested, with the APR and the CP as potential

candidates (Li et al, 2022; Liffner et al, 2023). One to three SPMTs in P. falciparum merozoites and 16 SPMTs in P. berghei sporozoites are attached to the APR. Interestingly, SPMTs are present, albeit perturbed, in SFA-deﬁcient parasites; in reverse, sporozoites lacking SPMTs still show the rootlet ﬁber (Spreng et al, 2019). Indeed, we could observe SPMTs in many anucleate merozoites, although they were fewer in number compared to SPMTs in nucleated merozoites. Similarly, sporozoites in SFA mutants showed fewer microtubules than in wildtype. Because SPMTs are nucleated early in segmentation and budding, the altered positioning and proximity of nuclei to the APRs inside the space-limited parasite could allow for the CP to nucleate and deliver the nascent SPMTs to the APR with a slightly lower efﬁciency. We also found lone microtubules in the sporoblasts of SFA mutants (Fig. EV5D), although nuclei appeared oriented with the CP facing the budding sites as in wildtype. Together, these data suggest that SFAs inﬂuence SPMT formation and/or stability either directly or indirectly, e.g., via their role in maintaining CP connection to the nascent apical ends of daughter cells. However, more work is needed to unambiguously show the origin of SPMT nucleation. Other organelles that require partitioning into merozoites and sporozoites and have previously been linked to the nucleus include the apicoplast and mitochondrion (Kudryashev et al, 2010; Schrevel et al, 2008; Verhoef et al, 2024). However, our data in merozoites show that their inheritance can occur in the absence of a nucleus, implying that their partitioning and/or maintenance mechanisms do not absolutely require a connection to the nucleus/CP. This suggests that the function of the SFA rootlet ﬁber, and to a certain degree the CP, is speciﬁc to nuclear division and structures that require spatial anchoring to the apical complex of the merozoite, such as rhoptries and SPMTs, and are less directly critical for mitochondrial and apicoplast maintenance in the daughter cells. Inside SFA-mutant oocysts, the few anucleate sporozoite-like buds still contained a mitochondrion but lacked the apicoplast, suggesting that these organelles are packaged in different manners and may utilize different inheritance mechanisms compared to the blood stage. The rootlet ﬁber thus emerges as an upstream component necessary to assemble parasites, but other components must also be present to secure full packaging of all organelles into budding sporozoites. How these organelles are trafﬁcked is still unclear. Another curious ﬁnding in oocysts lacking SFAs is a wide spreading of the IMC across the sporoblast membrane in a manner reminiscent of parasites lacking circumsporozoite protein (CSP) (Thathy et al, 2002). The IMC may thus serve as a secondary organizing principle, potentially by binding organelles, as has been previously suggested (Kudryashev et al, 2010). The higher aspect ratio (length vs. width) of the sporozoite (around 10) compared to the merozoite (around 2) might thus contribute to the stronger developmental arrest in sporozoites. The similarities and differences in phenotype due to the absence of the rootlet ﬁber between merozoites and sporozoites not only expand the role of SFAs and CP in regulating cell division more broadly but also underscore the architectural variations in cell division mechanisms across different life-cycle stages. Further studies are needed to distinguish whether SFAs play an active or passive role during the segmentation or budding of merozoites and sporozoites. Considering the broader parasite life cycle, we also surveyed the sexual developmental stages from gametocytogenesis to ookinete formation in P. berghei. These investigations corroborated our hypothesis that gametocyte formation and sexual commitment would be minimally affected by SFA mutants because nuclear inheritance does not take place. Interestingly, our data suggest a role for SFAs in efﬁcient male gametogenesis, subsequent ookinete conversion, and oocyst formation. These are all stages that require movement of the nucleus within the cell. Alternatively, the SFAs may function in the basal body of the male gamete in a manner similar to Chlamydomonas to contribute to successful and efﬁcient exﬂagellation and zygote formation. Recently, a study identiﬁed a protein, Calcifer, that keeps the basal body physically intact (Guan et al, 2026), and SFAs might play a similar role in basal body anchorage. This could be investigated with V5-tagged SFAs in the future as the GFP-tagged PbSFAs revealed no speciﬁc signal in gametocytes. Ookinetes inside the mosquito midgut undergo extensive cytoskeletal remodeling. Whether SFAs contribute to this process remains to be investigated, but they may be involved in nuclear positioning or apical complex formation, though likely to a lesser degree since oocyst formation is not majorly affected. In addition, the SFA1 mutants in both species of Plasmodium impart slightly more severe phenotypes across different life-cycle stages than their SFA2 counterparts, suggesting that SFA2 may have a stronger compensatory ability to support partial ﬁber formation. Alternatively, SFA1 may play a more important function in ﬁber biogenesis, which is supported by the appearance of the prominent, long, and thick striated structure inside the buds of PbSFA2-KO oocysts (Fig. 8F). Studying asexual replication that occurs inside the vertebrate liver would likely produce compelling companion data for our blood-stage ﬁndings. However, because SFAs are essential for sporozoite formation, stage-speciﬁc inducible KO or expression of SFAs under a sporogenesis-speciﬁc promoter would be required to interrogate their function during the liver stage. Since parasites undergo a similar albeit distinct process of schizogony in the liver compared to the intraerythrocytic version, we hypothesize that SFAs are also important during this stage (Roques et al, 2023). Overall, the SFA function linking the CP and forming daughter cells presented in this study is likely conserved across Plasmodium species and across replicative stages inside the vertebrate liver, RBCs, and mosquito midgut. A recent study in T. gondii has revealed novel proteins colocalizing with the SFA rootlet ﬁber: TgSFA4 (TGGT1_293170/ PF3D7_1447800), TgSFA5 (TGGT1_212780), and TGGT1_246740/PF3D7_1346000 (Li et al, 2024b). TgSFA5 was found to be essential for daughter cell formation, but it is a Sarcocystidae-speciﬁc protein. TgSFA4 and TGGT1_246740 both

have homologs in Plasmodium. We also investigated interactors of the SFA rootlet ﬁber in P. falciparum schizonts using PfSFA2 as a co-IP bait. The TgSFA4 ortholog was identiﬁed in our co-IP data but predicted to be dispensable (Dataset EV1) (Zhang et al, 2018). Beyond PfSFA1, which appeared as a top hit, this study also focused on two putative interactors of PfSFA2 – PF3D7_0703600 and PfPEARL. Both localized closely with PfSFA2 in schizonts— PF3D7_0703600 localized toward the basal end of the rootlet ﬁber, while PfPEARL localized toward the apical end. PF3D7_0703600 is a β-giardin-like protein with a similar protein size and predicted α- helical structure to alveolate SFAs. β-giardins belong to the larger SFA family proteins and have been shown to localize to the microtubule-associated Giardia ventral disc (Heiss et al, 2025; Nosala et al, 2020; Palm et al, 2005). Its role outside of Giardia is unknown, but our study presents initial evidence that PF3D7_0703600 may serve as an accessory protein to the SFA ﬁber, potentially as a linker between PfSFA2 and the outer-CP. Albeit limited, the evidence for this hypothesized function comes from the immunoﬂuorescence signal of PF3D7_0703600 overlapping with the outer-CP end of PfSFA2 and extending toward the nucleus. Its ortholog in P. berghei, PBANKA_0801300, may localize similarly, but detailed functional characterization in both species is needed to determine their speciﬁc role during schizogony and their relation to the SFA rootlet ﬁber. PfPEARL, on the other hand, seems to only be present in some primate Plasmodium species, and no obvious ortholog exists in P. berghei (Aurrecoechea et al, 2009). This protein partially colocalized with PfSFA2 during nascent apical pole generation and localized at the junction between the elongated SFA rootlet ﬁber and APR by the onset of segmentation. PfPEARL-KD had similar growth and morphological defects as PfSFA-KO—partial disconnection between the nuclei and forming merozoites, as well as dysregulated rhoptry formation. Rhoptries also seemed to aggregate in the residual body more often than in PfSFA-KO parasites. Strikingly, simultaneous depletion of PfPEARL and PfSFA2 led to a more severe segmentation defect and a complete arrest of bloodstage replication. Based on these ﬁndings, we hypothesize that PfPEARL is an accessory component of the SFA rootlet ﬁber and/or a linker between the ﬁber and the apical pole of forming daughter cells. In the absence of PfSFAs, PfPEARL may be able to partially maintain the connection between some of the nucleus-daughter cell pairs, and vice versa. PfPEARL may also occupy a distinct region between the rootlet ﬁber and the apical pole, as evidenced by its more apical localization prior to segmentation. This leads us to hypothesize that it may also play a more direct role in regulating rhoptry biogenesis, further supported by PfPEARL-deﬁcient schizonts exhibiting more severe dysregulation of rhoptry formation than PfSFA-deﬁcient parasites. An orthologous region contributing to APR-rootlet connection may also exist in P. berghei, but the lack of PfPEARL in the genome suggests that there are differences in the composition of SFA accessory proteins between these species. Other accessory proteins serving PfPEARLlike function may also exist, since the KD of PfPEARL alone did not completely ablate the formation of the SFA ﬁber between the outer- CP and APR (Fig. EV3). Therefore, studying other uncharacterized proteins pulled down with PfSFA2 (Dataset EV1) is necessary to resolve this apical connection more completely and further delineate the function of SFAs at the apical tip of the forming daughter cells.

Finally, the absence of SFAs in vertebrates and their divergent and central function across several life-cycle stages of Plasmodium position them as bona ﬁde targets for antimalarial intervention. Compounds that destabilize SFA ﬁbers or interfere with their interaction with the CP would disrupt parasite development at multiple bottlenecks, including blood-stage replication and sporozoite formation. Overall, we have demonstrated a signiﬁcant role that SFAs play in daughter cell formation across the Plasmodium life cycle. The use of P. falciparum and P. berghei allowed us to leverage the complementary strengths of each system: high-resolution characterization of SFA localization and function during human blood-stage replication in P. falciparum, and genetic interrogation of SFA function during experimentally tractable mosquito-stage development in P. berghei. Although this division necessarily limits direct comparisons across life-cycle stages and species, the concordance of SFA localization and perturbation phenotypes supports a conserved role for the SFA rootlet ﬁber during replicative stages. By connecting the CP with the apical pole of forming daughter cells, the SFA rootlet ﬁber ensures that each daughter cell faithfully receives one copy of the nucleus, and that its apical complex properly forms. Future work should focus on delineating the complete molecular composition of SFA rootlet ﬁber and CP, as well as the signaling pathways that regulate their dynamics.

Phylogenetic tree

A maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree of eight SFA orthologs in Plasmodium falciparum, P. berghei, Toxoplasma gondii, and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii were constructed in MEGA X using the JTT substitution model. Female Swiss CD1 mice (>20 g) obtained from Janvier Laboratories were used for generating mutant P. berghei parasites and propagating parasites for analysis. P. berghei strain ANKA parasites were used as a background to generate mutant lines and for control infections. Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes, reared in the dedicated insectary at Heidelberg University, were used for all P. berghei experiments.

Generation of transgenic P. falciparum parasite lines

Transgenic P. falciparum lines were generated using the CRISPR- Cas9 gene-editing system encoded on the sgRNA plasmids. HDR template and corresponding sgRNA plasmids were linearized with restriction enzymes, precipitated, then resuspended in transfectionready solutions followed by electroporation. To transfect into ringstage parasites, 100 μg of HDR plasmid and 50 μg of each guide plasmid (two guides at 100 μg total) were used and resuspended in 400 μL cytomix. To transfect into schizonts, 20 μg of each plasmid were used and resuspended in 15 μL sterile water. For ring-stage transfections, resuspended DNA is directly mixed with parasite culture before electroporation. For schizont transfections, the P3 Primary Cell 4D-Nucleofector® X Kit L was used, and electroporation was done with the Lonza 4D-Nucleofector instrument. After transfection, parasites were allowed to recover without selection for a day before adding appropriate drug(s), and the culture was monitored regularly before stable transgenic lines were established. Clonal lines were generated by limiting dilution and used for analysis for all replication assays and most biological replicates of microscopy experiments. Correct genetic modiﬁcations were veriﬁed by PCR analysis. Transgenic strains generated are described in detail in Table EV2.

P. falciparum replication assay

Replication assays were performed by synchronizing parasite cultures and assessing parasitemia at the young-ring stage using BD FACSCalibur or BD Accuri™C6 Plus Flow Cytometer every other day for 4 days (day 0 for only one biological replicate, day 2, and day 4 for all three biological replicates). Parasites were synchronized by pelleting schizonts with 60% percoll solution in PBS, followed by 5% (w/v) sorbitol treatment 2–4 h later. The parasites were then allowed to recover for 1–2 replicative cycles prior to harvesting. For knockdown (KD) experiments involving PfPEARL, ATc washout occurred either after percoll-pelleting of late-stage schizonts 4–6 h prior to harvesting early rings without sorbitol treatment, or after sorbitol treatment of early rings (4–6 h post invasion, hpi). In both cases, cultures were washed 2x with 10-min incubation each in complete media to remove ATc (inducing KD). For all experiments, early ring-stage cultures were harvested and equally split into individual tubes per condition, each containing 0.25% parasitemia and 1% hematocrit, and adding the modulatory drugs required for each condition, such as DMSO (vector control for inducible knockout, iKO), rapamycin (KO condition), or

P. falciparum immunoﬂuorescence microscopy, expansion microscopy, and image acquisition

For standard immunoﬂuorescence assay, parasites were harvested either on a microscope slide by smear-drying or on a poly-D lysinetreated 12 mm round coverslip (#1.5) by incubating culture on the coverslip for 30 min, then ﬁxed with prewarmed 4% (paraformaldehyde) PFA/PBS solution for 10–20 min, washed 3x with PBS for 3 min each, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton x-100 in PBS for 10 min, washed again with PBS 3x for 3 min each, then incubated with 3% (w/v) BSA/ PBS solution for 1 h to block. After blocking, speciﬁc primary antibodies diluted in 3% BSA/PBS solution (Table EV1) were incubated with the samples at 4 °C overnight. The next day, samples were washed in PBS 3x for 3 min each, then incubated with ﬂuorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies diluted in 3% BSA/ PBS (Table EV1) for 45 min, followed by another 3 × 3-min washes and incubation with Hoechst diluted in PBS. Quick 3x washes were performed before mounting the slide with a square coverslip, or the round coverslip onto a microscope slide, with 6–8 μL of VectaShield Vibrance mounting media. Mounting media was allowed to dry for 1–2 h before storing at 4 °C, and the slide was imaged the next day. Ultrastructure expansion microscopy was performed as previously described (Morano et al, 2024). All diluted reagents, including PBS, were made in Milli-Q (MQ) water. Schizont pellets were isolated by Percoll and incubated for 20–30 min on poly-D-lysine-treated 12 mm round coverslips (#1.0). To visualize mitochondria, schizonts were incubated with diluted MitoTracker Orange CMTMRos for 35 min while parasites settled on the coverslip. After harvesting, parasites were ﬁxed with prewarmed 4% PFA/PBS solution for 20 min at 37 °C, then gently washed 3x with prewarmed PBS followed by overnight 37 °C incubation in 1.4% formaldehyde and 2% acrylamide solution in PBS to prevent protein crosslinking. The next day, specimens were embedded in acrylamide gel, then denatured in buffer containing 200 mM SDS, 200 mM NaCl, and 50 mM Tris in MQ water with pH 9 at 95 °C for 90 min. The denatured gel was then expanded with MQ water 3x for 30 min. Following expansion, the gel was shrunk by incubation in PBS 2x for 15 min, then blocked with 3% BSA/PBS for 30 min. Then, a piece of the gel was excised and stained with speciﬁc primary antibodies diluted in 3% BSA/PBS (Table EV1) at 4 °C overnight. The following day, gels were washed 3x with PBS containing 0.5% Tween-20 for 10 min each, followed by a 2.5-h incubation with ﬂuorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies, NHS ester-conjugated ﬂuorescent dye, and SYTOX diluted in PBS (Table EV1). Gels were washed again for 3x with 0.5% Tween-20/PBS solution and underwent a second round of expansion in MQ water before they were ready for imaging. A piece of the expanded gel was excised and placed on a poly-

D lysine-covered dish for imaging. For most U-ExM experiments involving PfPEARL localization, ultracentrifugation (UC) followed by ﬁltration of primary and

DyLight secondary antibodies were performed to reduce background ﬂuorescence. First, antibodies were diluted according to the U-ExM protocol above, except the concentrations were increased twofold (e.g., 1:250 for secondary antibodies), and the plastic UC tubes were balanced and sealed. Ultracentrifugation was performed in a chilled vacuum (4 °C) at 50,000 RPM for 1 h. The antibody supernatant was then centrifuged through a 300 kDa ﬁlter (MWCO) at 15,000 × g for 10 min, and the eluate was used for antibody incubation. All images were acquired with Zeiss LSM900 with Airyscan2 for super-resolution microscopy, using the 63X oil objective with a numerical aperture of 1.4 or a 40X water objective with a numerical aperture of 1.2. Images were acquired with reasonable laser power between 0.1 and 4.5 and digital gain between 750 and 850. For experiments comparing speciﬁc signals between +DMSO and +Rapa parasites, the same laser power for the implicated channel was used for both conditions.

P. falciparum ﬂuorescence microscopy image processing

Z-stack images acquired using a Zeiss LSM900 microscope with Airyscan2 were ﬁrst processed through the ZEN software using built-in Airyscan Processing (AP) or Airyscan Joint Deconvolution (jDCV) features. Using the 63X objective, Z-stacks were acquired with 0.13-μm intervals for AP and 0.10-μm intervals for jDCV (20 maximum iterations and 0.1 quality threshold). Only the PfPEARL- KD/PfSFA2-iKO quantiﬁcation experiment utilized the 40X objective, and Z-stacks were acquired with 0.16-μm intervals for both AP and jDCV (same settings as with 63X). Processed images were then analyzed using FIJI. For all datasets, unless otherwise stated in the ﬁgure legends, image brightness and contrast were adjusted uniformly by applying the “Reset” (auto-scale) command in the Brightness/Contrast panel. This function adjusts the display range to cover the full dynamic range of the pixel intensity values, ensuring the displayed images remain as close as possible to their unprocessed appearance. For image insets, channel intensity values follow the “auto-scaled” parent image.

P. falciparum KO and KD induction

For iKO experiments, DMSO or rapamycin were added to parasite culture between 44 hpi and 4 hpi of the next cycle. For KD experiments, ATc washout occurred after percoll-pelleting of latestage schizonts as described for replication assays, and ATc was added back immediately after for the WT condition, while the KD condition received no drug. In all cases, drugs remained in the culture until schizont harvest at least 44 h post drug addition.

Western blotting

Parasite-infected RBCs were treated with 0.05% (w/v) saponin and protease inhibitors (SIGMA FAST Protease Inhibitor Cocktail or

Pierce Protease Inhibitor Tablets) in PBS to lyse and release content. Proteins from parasite lysates were then separated by SDS- PAGE (4–20% Mini-PROTEAN® TGX™Precast Protein Gels), transferred to nitrocellulose membrane, then probed with speciﬁc antibodies against the epitope or proteins of interest (mouse anti- V5 and rabbit anti-histone H3). Detection was achieved using ﬂuorescently labeled secondary antibodies and imaging software. Median intensity was obtained for quantiﬁcation.

Immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry

PfSFA2-smV5 parasites and a parallel cytoplasmic control line (PF3D7_1419700-smV5 (Rudlaff et al, 2019)) were synchronized using percoll density gradient centrifugation followed by sorbitol treatment after reinvasion. Cultures were expanded and allowed to develop to ~2–3% schizontemia in 6–8 mL of RBCs. iRBCs were lysed using 0.05% saponin in PBS containing protease inhibitors (SIGMA FAST Protease Inhibitor Cocktail), and schizont pellets were washed and collected by centrifugation. Pellets were lysed on ice in RIPA buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8; 150 mM NaCl; 1% NP40; 0.5% sodium deoxycholate; 0.1% SDS; 1x protease inhibitor). Lysates were incubated for 30 min on ice, followed by two rounds of sonication at 15–20% amplitude for 30 s each. Insoluble material was cleared by centrifugation, and the resulting supernatant was incubated overnight at 4 °C with magnetic anti-V5 beads (MBL Anti-V5-tag magnetic beads, Product #M167-11). Beads were washed ﬁve times in RIPA buffer containing protease inhibitors, followed by two washes in PBS with protease inhibitors. Samples were then resuspended in 50 μL of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and submitted to the Harvard Mass Spectrometry Core for on-bead digestion and mass spectrometry analysis. Mass spectrometry data were analyzed by comparing total and unique peptide counts and sum intensities of proteins between the immunoprecipitates of PfSFA2-smV5 and the cytoplasmic control. Candidate interacting proteins were identiﬁed by ranking the total peptide count of the ﬁrst replicate from highest to lowest and prioritizing those consistently enriched in the two replicate experimental samples (Dataset EV1). PfSFA1, PfSFA2, and analyzed interactors are highlighted in yellow.

P. berghei in vivo blood stage growth assay

To measure the asexual blood stage growth rate for WT, PbSFA1- KO and PbSFA2-KO parasites, 100 iRBCs of each line were intravenously injected into the tail veins of four C57BL/6 mice. Progression of parasitemia was monitored via Giemsa-stained blood smears from day 3 post injection onwards until the mice were either able to clear the infection and stayed negative for a week or killed due to showing symptoms of experimental cerebral malaria (ECM) or severe anemia. Parasitemia on day 7 after infection for WT and day 8 after injection for KOs were used to calculate the parasite multiplication rate (PMR), as the average fold-increase in parasitemia in two consecutive asexual cycles.

To analyze gametocytes, blood from mice infected with the respective parasite strains was collected once parasitemia exceeded 1%. and 2 × 10⁷ parasites were transferred into a recipient mouse by i.p. injection. Three days later, the presence of male gametocytes was assessed by phase-contrast microscopy at 40X magniﬁcation (exﬂagellation) after incubating a drop of blood on a glass slide covered by a coverslip for 13 min at 21 °C. Exﬂagellation centers were quantiﬁed across 30 randomly selected ﬁelds of view (FOVs) with the density of RBCs for normalization, and red blood cell density was determined in the ﬁrst FOV to normalize exﬂagellation rates. Additionally, the gametocytemia and parasitemia of the infected mice was counted using Giemsa-stained, blinded, thin blood smears. Ookinete conversion and motility assays

For in vitro maturation of ookinetes, blood was collected from infected mice once parasitemia reached 1%. A total of 2 × 10⁷ parasites were injected intraperitoneally into a recipient mouse, and 3 days later, the mice were sacriﬁced, and the collected blood was transferred into T-175 culture ﬂasks containing 10 mL ookinete medium. Ookinete medium consisted of RPMI-1640 supplemented with hypoxanthine (0.05 mg mL−¹), xanthurenic acid (100 μM), penicillin–streptomycin (1×), and 20% (v/v) FCS, with the pH adjusted to 7.8–8.0 using NaOH. Cultures were incubated for 20–24 h at 19 °C to allow ookinete maturation. Ookinetes were puriﬁed using a Nycodenz gradient. Cultures were transferred to 50 mL Falcon tubes and carefully underlaid with 8–9 mL 63% Nycodenz/PBS and centrifuged for 25 min at 500 × g without brake. Ookinetes were collected from the interphase, transferred to 15 mL Falcon tubes, and pelleted at 800 × g for 5 min. For motility assays, pellets were further centrifuged at 5000 × g for 3 min, resuspended in residual medium, and immediately used for imaging. Additionally, thin Giemsa-stained smears were prepared from the ookinete pellet (three technical replicates per two biological replicates) and analyzed using a Zeiss Axiostar Plus microscope until at least 60 zygotes were identiﬁed and counted per smear, as well as all ookinetes in the corresponding FOVs. For live motility analysis, 2 μL of resuspended ookinetes were mounted on glass slides under tightly sealed coverslips to ensure substrate contact on both sides. Time-lapse imaging was performed using a Zeiss Axiovert wideﬁeld microscope with a 25X objective. Movies were acquired over 5 min at 15-s intervals, and ookinete speed was quantiﬁed using the TrackMate plugin in Fiji (ImageJ2 version 2.16.0/1.54p), with identical detection and tracking parameters applied across all experiments.

Electron microscopy

To prepare samples for transmission electron microscopy, infected midguts from female mosquitoes were dissected at 12-, 15-, and 18- days post infection, and those midguts selected showed a high infection. The whole ﬁxation and embedding process was performed in the microwave (BioWave Pro+, Ted Pella Inc, Redding, CA, USA), and samples were cooled on ice when being microwaved. Midguts were chemically ﬁxed in 4% PFA & 1% glutaraldehyde in 100 mM PHEM buffer (60 mM PIPES, 25 mM HEPES, 10 mM EGTA, and 2 mM MgSO4) at 20 Hg vacuum and 100 Watts power for 8 min (with 2 min break every 2 min, so in total 14 min). Samples were washed twice in 100 mM PHEM buffer by microwaving samples at 250 W for 1 min. A secondary ﬁxation was done in 1% osmium tetroxide (in 100 mM PHEM buffer) at 20 Hg vacuum and 100 W for 8 min (with 2 min break every 2 min). Osmium tetroxide was removed by washing the sample twice in distilled water at 250 W for 1 min. Samples were then contrasted with 1% uranyl acetate (in ddH2O) for 8 min (with 2 min break every 2 min) at 20 Hg vacuum and 100 Watts. Samples were washed twice with distilled water as before and dehydrated for 40 s at 250 Watts in increasing concentrations of aqueous acetone (30%, 50, 70, and 90) and twice in 100% dried acetone. Samples were transferred to Spurr’s solution [23.6% epoxycyclohexyl- methyl- 3,4- epoxycyclohexylcarboxylate (ERL), 14.2% ERL- 4206 plasticizer, 61.3% nonenylsuccinic anhydride, 0.9% dimethylethanolamine] by being immersed in increasing concentrations of Spurr resin (25, 50, 75% in acetone) for 3 min each at 20 Hg vacuum and 250 W and ﬁnally immersed in 100% Spurr resin for 3 min at 20 Hg vacuum and 250 W. Samples were then immersed in 100% Spurr resin at room temperature overnight and polymerized afterward at 60 °C for at least 48 h. Embedded midguts were sectioned using an ultramicrotome (LEICA EM UC7, Leica Microsystems GmbH). About 1-μm-thick sections were collected for toluidine blue staining to check for oocysts in the current cutting plane. About 80- to 100-nm-thick single sections were acquired for 2D imaging, and 200-nm-thick serial sections were acquired for electron tomography. Sections were imaged on a transmission electron microscope at 200 kV (FEI Tecnai F20, FEI, Eindhoven, Netherlands) using an Eagle 4k × 4k CCD camera (FEI Eindhoven, Netherlands) using SerialEM version 4.1.18(Mastronarde, 2005).

Electron tomography

For tomography, bidirectional single-axis tilt series were taken from −60° to +60° with 2° increments. Tilt series of WT, SFA1KO and SFA2KO budding initiation, and WT and SFA1KO budding elongation were taken at 11,500X magniﬁcation resulting in a pixel size of 0.953 nm. A tilt series of SFA2KO budding elongation were taken at 9600X, resulting in a pixel size of 1.12 nm. Tilt series

were reconstructed into tomograms and joined into larger volumes using IMOD (Kremer et al, 1996). Eventually, three volumes were joined to a thickness of about 800 nm for budding initiations and three volumes of about 1.5 μm for budding elongations. Since this does not account for beam-induced shrinkage, the original depth covered may be greater. Segmentation of the cellular structures and visualization in 3D were performed using IMOD after isotropic binning by a factor of 2 to reduce ﬁle size.

Ethics statement

Animal experiments were performed according to Federation of European Laboratory Animal Science Associations (FELASA) and Society of Laboratory Animal Science (GV-SOLAS) guidelines and approved by the responsible German authorities (Regierungsprä- sidium Karlsruhe). Mice were obtained from Charles River Laboratories and kept in the dedicated animal facility of Heidelberg University according to current guidelines (3 mice per cage, ad libitum food and water, environmentally enriched cages).

Quantiﬁcation and statistical analysis

Unless otherwise indicated, at least three independent replicate experiments were conducted for experiments presented in the main ﬁgures. Data analysis and visualization were performed using the statistical software GraphPad Prism. Quantitative data were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or standard error of the mean (SEM). Differences between groups were assessed using appropriate statistical tests, including Mann–Whitney U-test, Fisher’s exact test, as well as one and two-way ANOVA, with corrections for multiple comparisons where appropriate. Figure legends contain details regarding speciﬁc statistical analyses performed. Statistical signiﬁcance was deﬁned as p < 0.05.

# Article

# In situ architecture of Opa1-dependent mitochondrial cristae remodeling

Michelle Y Fry1,2,14, Paula P Navarro1,2,11,14, Pusparanee Hakim 1, Virly Y Ananda1, Xingping Qin 3,4,5, Juan C Landoni 6, Sneha Rath1, Zintis Inde 3,4,5, Camila Makhlouta Lugo 1, Bridget E Luce1, Yifan Ge 1,2,12, Julie L McDonald 1,13, Ilzat Ali1,2, Leillani L Ha7,8, Benjamin P Kleinstiver7,8,9, David C Chan 10, Kristopher A Sarosiek3,4,5 & Luke H Chao 1,2✉

# Abstract

Cristae membrane state plays a central role in regulating mitochondrial function and cellular metabolism. The protein Optic atrophy 1 (Opa1) is an important crista remodeler that exists as two forms in the mitochondrion, a membrane-anchored long form (l-Opa1) and a processed short form (s-Opa1). The mechanisms for how Opa1 inﬂuences cristae shape have remained unclear due to lack of native three-dimensional views of cristae. We perform in situ cryo-electron tomography of cryo-focused ion beam milled mouse embryonic ﬁbroblasts with deﬁned Opa1 states to understand how each form of Opa1 inﬂuences cristae architecture. In our tomograms, we observe a variety of cristae shapes with distinct trends dependent on s-Opa1:l-Opa1 balance. Increased l-Opa1 levels promote cristae stacking and elongated mitochondria, while increased s-Opa1 levels correlated with irregular cristae packing and round mitochondria shape. Functional assays indicate a role for l-Opa1 in wild-type apoptotic and calcium handling responses, and show a compromised respiratory function under Opa1 imbalance. In summary, we provide three-dimensional visualization of cristae architecture to reveal relationships between mitochondrial ultrastructure and cellular function dependent on Opa1-mediated membrane remodeling.

# Introduction

Mitochondria play essential roles in energy production, metabolism and signaling, which drive diverse biological functions and processes of the cell (Chandel, 2014; Spinelli and Haigis, 2018; Picard and Shirihai, 2022). The organelle undergoes membrane remodeling during homeostatic steady-state conditions through fusion and ﬁssion to generate a dynamic and responsive reticulum (Twig et al, 2008; Mishra et al, 2014; Mishra and Chan, 2016). Mitochondrial ultrastructure is deﬁned by a double-membrane architecture with an outer (OMM) and inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). The IMM can be divided into three subregions, the cristae folds, the inner boundary membrane (IBM) and the cristae junctions (CJ), which separates cristae from the IBM. Cristae are enriched with electron transport chain (ETC) proteins, making them a hub for energy production (Schägger and Pfeiffer, 2000). In metazoans, cristae are mostly lamellar or tubular (Hashimi, 2019) and undergo dramatic rearrangements in response to stress and during initiation of apoptotic cell death (Frey and Mannella, 2000; Mannella, 2006; Zick et al, 2009). Despite longstanding interest in mitochondrial morphogenesis and major advances in understanding of mitochondrial structure and function (Friedman and Nunnari, 2014), regulation of cristae remodeling remains poorly understood. Relevant proteins for cristae remodeling include ATP synthase (Blum et al, 2019), optic atrophy protein 1 (Opa1) and the mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system (MICOS) (Friedman and Nunnari, 2014; Laan et al, 2016). Opa1 is responsible for fusing the IMM during mitochondrial fusion and is also implicated in cristae remodeling. Inner-membrane proteases, such as Oma1, Yme1L, and ParI, process Opa1 to generate a “soluble” form that lacks the N-terminal transmembrane (TM) segment (s-Opa1) (Song et al, 2007; Anand et al, 2014). This processing results in two forms of Opa1 in the mitochondria: the

We previously showed that stoichiometric levels of both l- and s-Opa1 are required for fast and efﬁcient membrane fusion in vitro (Ge et al, 2020); however, in situ ultrastructural understanding of how cristae shape is maintained by each Opa1 form is lacking. Previous work used transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging of chemically ﬁxed and heavy metal-stained cells to investigate the role of Opa1 in cristae shape. Knocking-down Opa1 induced more disorganized, globular and hyper-convex cristae, whereas over expression of Opa1 resulted in narrower cristae and CJs (Frezza et al, 2006). Initial steps of apoptosis involve release of cytochrome c from the cristae lumen, where ~85% of the cellular cytochrome c is stored (Scorrano et al, 2002). Expression of wild-type (WT) Opa1 was reported to protect against apoptosis by restricting cytochrome c release, whereas the loss of Opa1 was reported to result in mitochondria fragmentation and enhanced cytochrome c release (Scorrano et al, 2002). Addition of pro-apoptotic peptides resulted in wider CJs observed in TEM images. These observations suggest the organelle’s inner-membrane functional state may be sensitive to the levels of Opa1 present, and the membrane architectures supported by Opa1. To understand the role of s- and l-Opa1 in cristae architecture and remodeling, we investigated the in situ state of mitochondrial membranes in mouse embryonic ﬁbroblasts (MEF) with different levels of s- and l-Opa1, by applying cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) on cryo-focused ion beam (cryo-FIB) milled MEF. We used deﬁned cell lines that predominantly contained either lor s-Opa1 to characterize how mitochondrial membrane organization and shape depend on the expression levels and form of Opa1. Here, we present an extensive characterization of the 3D morphological properties of mitochondrial cristae membranes. We observed that l-Opa1 contributes to crista stacking, longer cristae, a reduction of globular cristae, an absence of tubular cristae and the maintenance of cristae junction widths. We found that the presence of s-Opa1 correlates with tubular cristae, wider cristae junctions, narrower cristae, and irregular cristae packing. Using BH3 proﬁling, we observed WT-like apoptotic responses only in the cells with l-Opa1. We also found WT-like calcium handling responses in cells expressing mainly l-Opa1 and that both forms of Opa1 are important for normal respiratory function. Our work reveals roles for s- and l-Opa1 beyond mitochondrial fusion and demonstrates that both forms of Opa1 play distinct roles in cristae shape maintenance important for mitochondrial function.

## Results

In situ morphology of mitochondria with different Opa1 processing

We generated cryo-electron tomograms of mitochondria from cryo-FIB milled MEF cell lines that differed in the expression levels and processed states of Opa1, to investigate mitochondrial cristae ultrastructure (Appendix Fig. S1). In this study, we used ﬁve MEF cell lines: (i) wild-type (WT) cells, (ii) cells stably overexpressing Opa1 (Opa1-OE), (iii) a Δexon5b CRISPR MEF line with an oma1-/-

background, which restricts Opa1 cleavage and results in the

presence of mostly l-Opa1 (referred to as l-Opa1* in this work), (iv) an Opa1 knock-out (Opa1-KO) line stably expressing the Opa1 isoform 5, which is robustly processed and results in the presence of s-Opa1 (referred to as s-Opa1*) and (v) Opa1-KO cells (Mishra et al, 2014; Wang et al, 2021; Appendix Fig. S1). While previous studies have characterized mitochondrial ultrastructure, these samples were subjected to chemical ﬁxation and heavy metal staining, which are recognized to perturb cellular membrane state and limit resolution (Bäuerlein and Baumeister, 2021). Thus, we vitriﬁed MEF cell lines to characterize mitochondrial membrane architecture under native conditions. To prepare samples for cryo- ET imaging, we generated ~200-350 nm thick lamellae by cryo-FIB milling (Rigort et al, 2012; Mahamid et al, 2016), following a previously established imaging pipeline (Navarro et al, 2022). A total of 100 tilt-series (WT = 33, Opa1-OE = 7, l-Opa1* = 21, s- Opa1* = 28 and Opa1-KO = 11) were acquired, aligned and threedimensionally (3D) reconstructed into tomograms (Table EV1). Cryo-electron tomograms were denoised using Topaz-Denoise to improve mitochondrial membrane visualization (Bepler et al, 2020). It is important to note that cryo-electron tomograms generated by cryo-FIB milling cover a section of the mitochondria contained within the thickness of the lamella, thus, all mitochondria were partially imaged in the Z-axis. In some cases, mitochondria are only partially visible in the XY plane due to the trade-off between resolution and ﬁeld of view (Navarro, 2022; Appendix Fig. S2A). Densities corresponding to the IMM and OMM were 3D segmented in yellow and green, respectively (Fig. 1A, Movies EV1–5). The generated tomograms provide rich 3D information on mitochondrial morphology. By visual morphological analysis, we classiﬁed mitochondria into ellipsoidal, round, partial (when partially imaged in the XY plane) or polygon shape categories. The majority of mitochondria in all cell lines are ellipsoidal, except for s-Opa1* cells, where round mitochondria dominate (Fig. 1B), correlating with a smaller apparent mitochondrial area (Fig. 1C). Mitochondria in WT cells are larger in area (0.34 ± 0.03 µm2) than in other cell lines; with smaller mitochondria in l-Opa1* cells (0.2 ± 0.02 µm2) and signiﬁcantly smaller mitochondria in Opa1-OE (0.14 ± 0.02 µm2) and s-Opa1* cells (0.18 ± 0.02 µm2) (Fig. 1C). We measured the mitochondrial volume and the volumes of each subcompartment: the matrix, inner membrane space (IMS) and cristae lumen (CL) (Fig. EV1). Our analysis shows that imbalance of l- and s-Opa1 levels results in larger CL volume (Fig. EV1C–F). At ﬁrst glance, we observed differences in matrix contrast between mitochondria from different cell lines in our cryo-ET data. To investigate this further, we quantiﬁed the gray scale levels in normalized summed projected images from cryo-electron tomograms (Fig. EV1G). We observed denser mitochondrial matrices in Opa1-OE, l-Opa1*, and Opa1-KO mitochondria. For the Opa1-OE mitochondria, the darker measured gray scale value can be attributed to the presence of electron dense deposits within the mitochondrial matrix, likely to be calcium phosphate deposits (Wolf et al, 2017; Strubbe-Rivera et al, 2021; Figs. 1A and S2A white arrowheads, Fig. EV1H). We analyzed mitochondrial cristae density (number of cristae/ µm2) in the cryo-electron tomograms. No signiﬁcant difference was observed in the cristae density between mitochondria in WT and Opa1-KO cells (Fig. EV2A). All other conditions (Opa1-OE,

In situ cristae ultrastructure

To address questions related to the speciﬁc roles for Opa1 forms in cristae morphology, we sought to characterize the dependence of cristae architecture on the form of Opa1 present. Based on their direction relative to the OMM, we quantiﬁed cristae as straight or tilted. For some cristae, no connection to the IMM was captured in the tomogram and thus classiﬁed as no attachment observed (NAO) (Fig. 2A). This is a consequence of all mitochondria being partially imaged in the z-axis, as mentioned above. In Opa1-KO cells fewer cristae were straight compared to WT (Fig. 2A). The presence of either form of Opa1 restores the proportion of straight cristae to WT-like levels, while overexpression of Opa1 results in more straight cristae than WT. Cristae were then classiﬁed based on 3D-shape into canonical lamellar, globular, and tubular categories (Harner et al, 2016). Across all cell lines, lamellar cristae dominate (Fig. 2B). Interestingly, the proportion of lamellar cristae increases in l-Opa1* (81%) and s-Opa1* (77%) cells. Tubular cristae are not observed in l-Opa1* and Opa1-KO cells and are reduced in Opa1-OE (3.24%) and s-Opa1* (2.3%) cells compared to WT (9.6%). Globular cristae are present in all cell lines albeit to a lesser extent when Opa1 expression levels are altered but increased in the absence of Opa1 (Fig. 2B). The proportion of unusually shaped cristae is similar among WT (27%) and Opa1-OE (30.52%), but reduced in l-Opa1* (17%), s-Opa1* (16.9%) and Opa1-KO (18.9%) cell lines (Fig. 2B, Appendix Fig. S2A). Unusual cristae were further subclassiﬁed into eight deﬁned categories: (i) loop, where cristae curve and connect to IBM via two CJs; (ii) split, where cristae branch into two or more cristae; (iii) straight-across, when cristae are perpendicular and connect to the IBM via two CJs; (iv) amorphous, when cristae display a nebulous morphology; (v) ring, where cristae are circular; (vi) pinched, where cristae show areas where membranes touch; (vii) zipped, when cristae have regions where both membranes merge until both cannot be distinguished; and (viii) vesicular, where material is observed within the cristae (Fig. EV4). Of these categories only ﬁve were observed in WT mitochondria—ring, loop, straight-across,

amorphous, and split. The loop phenotype is dominant in WT unusual cristae, but also present in all cell lines (Fig. EV4A). Pinched and zipped cristae are absent in WT cells but predominant in Opa1-OE cells. Zipped cristae were observed in l-Opa1* cells and only once in s-Opa1* cells, suggesting l-Opa1 may play a role in bridging the two membranes of the cristae for long stretches. In the absence of Opa1, no split or straight across cristae were observed; instead, more cristae fall into the amorphous and vesicular categories. An increase in amorphous cristae were also observed in l-Opa1* and s-Opa1* cells. All cristae shapes were observed in s-Opa1* cells, with roughly a quarter of the unusual cristae falling into the pinched category. Compared to WT, a similar proportion of unusual cristae in s-Opa1* mitochondria fall into the split category. Ring shaped cristae are rare and were not observed in l-Opa1* cells. To determine the dependence of cristae length and width on the form of Opa1 present, we measured in 3D the length and width of ﬁfty cristae per cell line (Appendix Fig. S3A). Knocking out Opa1 results in signiﬁcantly longer cristae (Fig. 2C). This increase in cristae length was not observed in Opa1-OE cells, but was observed in both s-Opa1* and l-Opa1* cells. In s-Opa1* mitochondria, there is a broad distribution of cristae lengths, with a considerable number of longer cristae than WT, which was also observed in Opa1-KO mitochondria. Overexpression of Opa1 does not affect cristae width, but the absence of Opa1 correlates with wider cristae, consistent with a larger proportion of observed globular cristae (Fig. 2D). Cristae widths are restored to WT values in l-Opa1* mitochondria, but in s-Opa1* mitochondria cristae are signiﬁ- cantly narrower. Though Opa1-OE and l-Opa1* mitochondria have similar average cristae widths to WT mitochondria, a larger variation in cristae widths was observed, with many values falling into 0-5 nm and 9-14 nm ranges (Fig. 2F,G). This suggests that a signiﬁcant proportion of cristae in Opa1-OE and l-Opa1* mitochondria vary in width, correlating with an increase in the number of zipped or pinched cristae in these cell lines (Fig. 2E). Even though cristae width histograms from s-Opa1* and WT mitochondria exhibit a single narrow peak, s-Opa1* mitochondria have tighter cristae (6–15 and 9–16 nm, respectively) (Fig. 2E–G). In Opa1-KO mitochondria, the cristae width distribution peak ranges from 10 to 17 nm, with an outlier representing a population of extremely wide cristae also seen in l-Opa1* mitochondria, particularly a subclass of globular cristae (Fig. 2B,D–G). These observations suggest the uniformity of cristae widths observed in WT mitochondria is disrupted by changes in Opa1 expression levels and suppression of Opa1 processing.

Cristae junction morphology by cryo-ET

To gain insight into the role of each Opa1 form at the cristae junction (CJ), we measured and analyzed CJs from summed projected central slices of tomograms for all cell lines. CJs were deﬁned as the site where the crista membrane joins the boundary region of the IMM (Appendix Fig. S3C). Compared to WT mitochondria, we observed wider CJs in Opa1-KO mitochondria, consistent with previous TEM data (Scorrano et al, 2002) and unaltered CJ widths in Opa1-OE mitochondria (Fig. 3A). Intriguingly, we found that CJs are also signiﬁcantly wider in s-Opa1* mitochondria compared to WT mitochondria (Fig. 3A). We did not, however, ﬁnd any signiﬁcant difference in CJ widths in l-Opa1* mitochondria. These measurements indicate under

steady-state conditions complete processing of Opa1 results in larger CJ widths. In our initial inspection of our tomograms, we noticed that a greater proportion of cristae in s-Opa1* mitochondria are tilted, i.e., where the crista length is not perpendicular to the IBM (Fig. 2A). To further investigate if this tilt occurs at the beginning of the crista or along the length of the cristae, we quantiﬁed the angle at the CJ (Appendix Fig. S3D). While most cristae are orthogonal to the OMM, we observed a wide range of CJ angles in s-Opa1* mitochondria. Overall, the CJ angles in s-Opa1* cristae are less perpendicular compared to WT CJs, demonstrating that the tilted cristae observed in these cells occurs at the CJ (Figs. 2A and 3B,C). Functional consequences of Opa1 state

We next examined the consequences of Opa1 levels and processing on mitochondrial function. First, we sought to uncover potential effects of Opa1 perturbation on the intrinsic apoptotic pathway. We used BH3 proﬁling to compare mitochondrial responses to proapoptotic stimuli across the cell lines. BH3 proﬁling quantiﬁes the percentage of cells that release cytochrome c from their mitochondria, the key commitment step in mitochondrial apoptosis, in response to treatment with BH3 peptides that mimic the activity of pro-apoptotic proteins from the BCL-2 family (Fraser et al, 2018). Cells that release cytochrome c in response to moderate or weak pro-apoptotic stimuli are considered to be primed for apoptosis, whereas cells that require strong stimuli to trigger cytochrome c release are unprimed. Apoptotic priming has been previously shown to determine whether healthy and cancerous cells undergo apoptosis in response to cellular stress or damage (Chonghaile et al, 2011; Sarosiek et al, 2017; Spetz et al, 2022). BH3 proﬁling showed a substantial reduction in apoptotic priming of Opa1-KO cells relative to WT cells as indicated by decreased sensitivity to the BIM BH3 peptide, which can inhibit all pro-survival Bcl-2 family proteins and directly activate BAX and BAK (Kale et al, 2018; Fig. 4A). Equal doses of the BIM BH3 peptide induced less cytochrome c release from mitochondria in Opa1-KO cells than WT cells, indicating that stronger pro-death stimuli are required to induce apoptosis in cells lacking Opa1 (Fig. 4A). We also tested MEF sensitivity to common apoptosis-inducing agents by quantifying positivity for Annexin V, which binds phosphatidylserine on the surface of cells undergoing early apoptosis, after treatment. Based on the BH3 proﬁling results, we would expect less apoptosis after treatment of Opa1-KO cells than WT cells. We found that indeed this was the case: Opa1-KO MEF were more resistant to treatment with the topoisomerase inhibitor etoposide, DNA damaging agent doxorubicin, and pan-kinase inhibitor staurosporine at 24 h (Fig. 4B). Similar differences in sensitivity were also detected at 48 and 72 h, suggesting that retention of cytochrome c durably protected Opa1 KO cells from commitment to apoptosis (Appendix Fig. S4). Overexpression of Opa1 maintains a WT-level response to apoptotic stimuli. While s-Opa1* cells show levels of apoptotic priming between WT and Opa1-KO cells, the short-form is not sufﬁcient to rescue normal apoptotic priming of MEF. In contrast, l-Opa1* cells behave similarly to the WT cells across most conditions, restoring apoptotic priming (Fig. 4A). These results suggest that these lines would not be as resistant to apoptosisinducing agents as the Opa1-KO cells and is evident in the 24-h chemosensitivity data for etoposide, doxorubicin, and staurosporine treatment (Fig. 4B) as well as data at 48- and 72-h posttreatment (Appendix Fig. S4). The presence of a stable l-Opa1

population has been previously shown to be essential in apoptotic resistance (Merkwirth et al, 2008, 2012). Our results indicate Opa1 processing is not required for apoptotic priming. In Opa1-KO or s- Opa1* cells, wider CJ at steady-state conditions correlated with cells resistant to apoptosis. To understand the impact of Opa1-dependent remodeling on mitochondrial calcium homeostasis and mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening, we performed mitochondrial calcium retention capacity (CRC) assay on MEF cell lines. Mitochondria from permeabilized l-Opa1* cells show similar CRC proﬁles to WT (Fig. 4C). In contrast, s-Opa1* cells and Opa1-KO cells are observed to be more resistant to mPTP opening (Fig. 4C,D) and require higher concentrations of CaCl2 to induce the pore opening transition (Fig. 4B). The presence of vesicular cristae and wider CJs at steady-state conditions correlate with s-Opa1* and Opa1-KO cells resistant to calcium-induced mPTP opening. In contrast, Opa1-OE cells undergo mPTP transition at lower amounts of CaCl2 stimulation. We note an elevated presence of mitochondrial calcium deposits in the Opa1-OE cell line (Fig. EV1H). Next, we evaluated the mitochondrial respiratory ﬁtness of all cell lines to assess how a key cristae-dependent function varies upon Opa1 perturbation. As previously observed, mitochondrial respiration is severely impaired in Opa1-KO cells (Zhang et al, 2011; Fig. 5A). Basal OCR levels for Opa1-OE cells are similar to WT (Fig. 5B). s-Opa1* and l-Opa1* cells both have basal oxygen consumption respiration (OCR) levels signiﬁcantly lower than WT, as previously reported (Lai et al, 2020; Lee et al, 2020). Cell lines with lower basal OCRs, also display signiﬁcantly lower maximal respiration and spare capacity levels (Fig. 5B). Longer cristae and more amorphous cristae were observed in these cell lines. These results suggest that balanced levels of both forms of Opa1 are required for normal mitochondrial respiration. Mitochondrial ﬁtness was also measured in the oma1-/- background in which the l-Opa1* cells were generated (Wang et al, 2021). Like l-Opa1* cells, oma1-/- cells also have WT levels of cytochrome c release upon treatment with BIM (Appendix Fig. S5A). Additionally, oma1-/- MEF cells show WT-like propensity for mPTP opening under Ca2+ stimulation albeit displaying a lower overall calcium buffering proﬁle than WT and l-Opa1* cells (Appendix Fig. S5B). OCR values in l-Opa1* cells are signiﬁcantly lower than in oma1-/- cells, indicating the OMA1 deletion is not the sole contributor to the impaired respiration observed in l-Opa1* cells (Appendix Fig. S5C,D). These data suggest that functional differences in the l-Opa1* mitochondria are dependent on the form of Opa1 present. Finally, we investigated the effect of Opa1 imbalance on mtDNA maintenance. Mitochondrial fusion is essential for maintaining mtDNA stability (Elachouri et al, 2011) and Opa1 depletion has been shown to lead to a decrease in mtDNA number and translation (Chen et al, 2010). Consistent with previous reports, we observed robust mtDNA decrease in Opa1-KO MEF quantiﬁed by instant Structured Illumination Microscopy (iSIM) imaging (Appendix Fig. S6A–C) and qPCR (Appendix Fig. S6D). Stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy studies in HeLa and human ﬁbroblast cells have shown that nucleoids occupy mitochondrial matrix spaces between clusters of cristae (Stephan et al, 2019) and when fusion is inhibited, nucleoids cluster without changes in size and copy number (Ramos et al, 2019). ## Discussion

Understanding how sophisticated membrane architectures are generated in pleiomorphic organelles poses a challenge and opportunity for structural cell biology. The mitochondrion is an exemplar case where the organelle’s morphology can take on a wide range of forms regulated by dynamic protein assemblies (Mageswaran et al, 2023). In

this work, we used state-of-the-art in situ cryo-ET to analyze how Opa1 processing regulates mitochondrial ultrastructure, in particular cristae morphology. Previous analyses of mitochondrial cristae morphology have been informed by conventional TEM micrographs of ﬁxed and heavy metal-stained cells known to perturb membrane structures and introduce imaging artifacts (Scorrano et al, 2002; Olichon et al, 2003; Frezza et al, 2006). In overcoming these limitations, we characterized and quantiﬁed a diverse range of cristae morphologies speciﬁc to the form of Opa1 present in the cell. Here, we discuss structure/function relationships which emerged from this study (Fig. 6). Our 3D data captures the diversity of cristae morphologies and can distinguish lamellar and tubular cristae. Recent single particle cryo-EM helical reconstructions of human s-Opa1 decorating the exterior of membranes tubes show how paddle domain interactions facilitate self-assembly (Malsburg et al, 2023; Nyenhuis et al, 2023). The increase in globular cristae in the Opa1-KO condition may imply that the presence of either or both forms of Opa1 support lamellar cristae. Indeed, a recent study found knock-down of Opa1 altered the ratio of lamellar to tubular cristae (Suga et al, 2023). Further integrative structural studies will also be necessary to directly relate how speciﬁc protein conformational states inﬂuence such morphologies (Fig. 6C; Harner et al, 2016). Visualizing mitochondrial membrane structure using cryo-ET enables us to make accurate measurements of membrane distances. l-Opa1* cells maintained WT-like CJ widths (Fig. 3A), which with our BH3 proﬁling assay suggest that l-Opa1 plays a role in maintaining CJ widths and mediating the response to apoptotic stimulation (Fig. 6D). TEM imaging showed that cytochrome c release (stimulated by pro-apoptotic signaling proteins such as BID) results in the widening of cristae junctions and opening of the cristae lumen (Scorrano et al, 2002; Frezza et al, 2006). In contrast to previous studies, we investigated cristae state prior to any exposure to extracellular stress or apoptotic stimuli (Merkwirth et al, 2008, 2012). Building upon previous studies, we observed wider cristae junctions in Opa1-KO and s-Opa1* cells prior to apoptotic initiation (Fig. 3). Together, with our apoptotic priming results demonstrating that cells lacking l-Opa1 released less cytochrome c upon apoptosis stimulation, our observations support a speciﬁc CJ regulatory role for l-Opa1 in the cytochrome c release transition (Fig. 6B,C; Merkwirth et al, 2008). Our ﬁndings that Opa1-KO cells are resistant to apoptosis may seem counterintuitive given previous reports of apoptotic resistance in Opa1-overexpressing cells (Frezza et al, 2006). roles for Opa1 during apoptotic membrane transitions. During apoptosis, Opa1 maintains cristae junctions, which may restrict cytochrome c release in response to pro-apoptotic signals (Frezza et al, 2006). However, the importance of rearrangement and disassembly of Opa1 complexes during apoptosis initiation, to facilitate CJ opening, as discussed above, demonstrates that Opa1 also has a direct role in the earlier steps when apoptosis is being initiated (Fig. 6D). This view is consistent with our ﬁnding that complete knock-out of Opa1 impairs cytochrome c release and can be protective against apoptosis-inducing agents (Fig. 4A,B). Our data indicate that apoptotic response is independent of Opa1 processing (Cipolat et al, 2006) and cytochrome c release is dependent on initial CJ widths. Our BH3 proﬁling results are supported by CRC assay results, where l-Opa1 presence in MEF allows for WT-like responses towards increased Ca2+ and apoptotic stimulation (Fig. 4C,D). These independent functional outcomes are connected by the importance of membrane integrity in mPTP opening (Strubbe- Rivera et al, 2021; Bernardi et al, 2023) and BAX/BAK-mediated cytochrome c cristae remodeling (Scorrano et al, 2002; Renault et al, 2015). Consistent with previous reports of calcium phosphate deposits, we observed dense deposits in the mitochondria matrix of most Opa1-OE mitochondria (Wolf et al, 2017), which correlates with a lower mPTP transition CaCl2 threshold. Cryo-ET enabled this ﬁnding and allows us to attribute differences in density in the mitochondrial matrix to biological material, and not artifacts from chemical agents. We note a less condensed matrix in mitochondria in s-Opa1* cells and a lighter matrix in the Opa1-KO mitochondria, which we speculate may be related to matrix components other than calcium. Our measurements also suggest that l-Opa1 may contribute to maintaining perpendicular CJ, as fewer perpendicular CJs were observed in s-Opa1* cells. Perpendicular CJs can facilitate cristae stacking, which we noticed in a striking number of l-Opa1* cells. Stacking cristae have been previously observed both under conditions that induce metabolic and endoplasmic reticulum stress upon addition of thapsigargin (Barad et al, 2022) and in oma1-/-

cells (Anand et al, 2014). We speculate that cristae stacking may have features in common to an intermediate preceding fusion (Fig. 6C). Consistent with this role, we also note a correlation between stacked cristae organization in the l-Opa1* cells facilitating mtDNA distribution. While Opa1-KO cells have a dramatic loss of mtDNA number, we still visualize the presence of cristae in these mitochondria. This further supports emerging evidence that the organization of multiple crista contribute to mtDNA maintenance (Stephan et al, 2019; Jakubke et al, 2021). We also assessed the effects of Opa1 state on mitochondrial respiration, a central function dependent on cristae shape (Cogliati et al, 2016). In short, compromised respiration observed in l- Opa1*, s-Opa1*, and Opa1-KO cells correlates with a larger percentage of amorphous cristae and longer cristae lengths. This suggests both forms of Opa1 play a role in maintaining a deﬁned cristae shape and length. Our work indicates more subtle cristae phenotypes (such as vesicular and amorphous) may also not be optimal for respiration (Fig. 6). We speculate disruption of cristae shape could destabilize respiratory complex assembly in the cristae membranes or vice versa. Future studies will be necessary to more directly link in situ mitochondrial ultrastructure with mitochondrial dysfunction.

In summary, here we characterize cristae morphologies related to the levels or forms of Opa1 present in the cell. We characterize and quantify cristae morphological differences and deﬁne distinct differences speciﬁc to each Opa1 form. Notably, we ﬁnd evidence that l-Opa1 plays important roles in maintaining CJ width and connectivity, which correlates well with WT-like apoptotic and calcium responses. We also demonstrate that both forms of Opa1 are required for maintaining cristae membrane shape and mitochondrial respiration, linking amorphous cristae with mitochondrial dysfunction. This work, in describing cristae morphology and functions, opens new opportunities for understanding mitochondrial ultrastructure and function, and motivates further studies visualizing and dissecting mechanisms underlying cristae heterogeneity by new live cell imaging approaches to gain insights into the spatio-temporal regulation of their lifecycle.

## Methods

Cell lines and culture

MEF were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin at 37 °C and 5% CO2. Wildtype and Opa1 knock-out MEF cell lines were purchased from ATCC. Δexon5b/oma1-/- cells and Opa1 knockouts transfected retrovirally with Opa1 Isoform 5 (KO Opa1 + Iso5) were kind gifts from David Chan (California Institute of Technology) (Song et al, 2007). The KO Opa1 + Iso5 were maintained in the same condition described above and supplemented with puromycin at 1 µg/mL. Cell genotypes were conﬁrmed by Western blotting. To mediate a constitutive overexpression of Opa1 from the safe harbor locus Rosa26 in MEF, mouse Opa1 sequence was cloned into pR26-CMVconst (Addgene plasmid #127373; http://n2t.net/addgene:127373; RRID: Addgene_127373; kind gift by Lance Miller) to generate pR26- CMV-Opa1 (pAH33). Following sequence veriﬁcation, the construct was co-transfected with pX330-sgR26 (Addgene plasmid #127376; http://n2t.net/addgene:127376; RRID: Addgene_127376; kind gift by Lance Miller) into WT MEF cells using Lipofectamine 3000. Transfected cells were selected with 5 µg/mL puromycin starting 24 h post-transfection for 7 days. Stable clones were expanded for 7 days, and their genotypes were conﬁrmed by Western blotting. Opa1-OE MEF cell line was cultured in the same manner described above, with the addition of 2.5 µg/mL puromycin in the culture media. Human HEK 293T cells (American Type Culture Collection; ATCC) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modiﬁed Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated FBS (HI-FBS) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Samples of supernatant media from cell culture experiments were analyzed monthly for the presence of mycoplasma using MycoAlert PLUS (Lonza). To generate a HEK 293T cell line bearing an OPA1 exon 5b knock-out, SpCas9 sgRNAs were cloned into pUC19-U6- BsmBI_cassette-SpCas9gRNA (BPK1520; Addgene ID 65777) harboring spacer sequences GCTCATTGTGAACTCGTGGCA (plasmid CJT90), GCCAACAGAAGCGCAAGGTGA (plasmid CJT91), GTTCTCCTCATTGTGAACTCG (plasmid CJT92), and GCAGAAGCGCAAGGTGATGGA (plasmid CJT93), each with added 5’Gs. Transfections were performed 20 h following seeding of 2 × 104 HEK 293T cells per well in 96-well plates and contained 70 ng of ABE8e plasmid and 30 ng of sgRNA expression plasmid mixed with 0.3 µL of TransIT- X2 (Mirus) in a total volume of 15 µL Opti-MEM (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc). The transfection mixtures were incubated for 15 min at room temperature and distributed across the seeded HEK 293T cells. Cells were grown for approximately 72 h prior to extracting gDNA as described above. Editing efﬁciency in bulk transfected cells was assessed by NGS using PCR round 1 primers oLLH7- ACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCTGCT TAGGCTGTTGACATCACTGGAGAATG and oLLH8-GACTG GAGTTCAGACGTGTGCTCTTCCGATCTCCAGAACTGCCAC GTAATACCTTGTAC. To create cell lines, HEK 293T cells were seeded and transfected with plasmids KAC984 and CJT88. Transfected cells were grown for approximately 72 h prior to dilution plating into 96-well plates and grown until conﬂuent. Cells were transferred into 24-well plates with some cell mass reserved to extract genomic DNA (gDNA) for genotyping via PCR and NGS to verify biallelic introduction of OPA1-R194G.

Live cell epiﬂuorescence microscopy

Conﬂuent MEF cells were harvested, seeded onto 35 mm glassbottom dishes (MatTek Life Sciences) coated with poly-D-lysine

(0.1 mg/mL) and allowed to grow overnight at 37 °C under 5% CO2. For visualization of mitochondria, cells were stained with 50 nM MitoTrackerTM Deep Red FM (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc) at 37 °C for 15 min. Following three rounds of washes with 1X PBS, cells were placed in Live Cell Imaging Solution (Invitrogen). Imaging relating to Fig. EV3 was performed using Zeiss Axio Observer Z1 Advanced Marianas™ Microscope system, an Alpha Plan- Apochromat ×100/1.46 NA Oil TIRF Objective M27 and Prime 95B scientiﬁc CMOS camera (Photometrics). MitoTrackerTMstained mitochondria were imaged using “Cy5” ﬁlter set (Cy5- 4040C, Excitation: 628/40 nm [608-648 nm], Emission: 692/40 nm [672–712 nm], Dichroic Mirror: 660 nm) (Semrock). Temperature, humidity, and CO2 concentrations were controlled with an Okolab Microscope Stage Incubator System. Image acquisition and processing were done using SlideBookTM6 (Intelligent Imaging Innovations, Inc., Denver, CO) and Fiji (Schindelin et al, 2012). Time-lapse videos of stained mitochondria were taken at one frame per 30 s for a duration of 5 min.

Fluorescence imaging and quantiﬁcation

To determine mitochondrial network morphology, MEF cells were seeded onto glass-bottom dishes and grown to ~80% conﬂuency. Cells were washed with PBS and ﬁxed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS for 20 mins. Following three washes with PBS, cells were permeabilized in 0.1% Triton X-100 diluted in PBS for 5 min. Cells were incubated in 2% normal goat serum and 0.05% Triton X-100 in PBS for 1 h, and subsequently incubated in the same buffer with 1:300 Tom20 Recombinant rabbit antibody (Invitrogen) overnight at 4 °C. After thorough washing with PBS, cells were incubated with 1:1000 goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor® 488 AfﬁniPure antibody (Jackson ImmunoResearch) for 1 h at RT. Cells were washed in PBS and coated with UltraCruz® Aqueous Mounting Medium with DAPI (Santa Cruz) prior to imaging. Images were captured using A1R HD25 point scanning confocal with GaAsP and PMT detectors, equipped with an Apo TIRF 60x/1.49 NA objective lens and Ti2 Z-drive. Cells were manually scored into four morphological classiﬁcations (Wang et al, 2021): “Fragmented” refers to cells that contain spherical mitochondrial fragments with two or less short tubules present. “Short tubular” refers to cells containing a mixture of fragmented and short tubular mitochondria. “Long tubular” refers to cells with elongated mitochondria, but not fused into a mitochondrial mesh. “Interconnected” refers to cells with a highly interconnected network of mitochondrial ﬁlaments, with few isolated mitochondria present.

Cryo-EM specimen preparation

Cells were prepared following the deposition method. Cells were detached and counted with a hemocytometer. Quantifoil 200 mesh holey carbon R2/2 (EMS) were glow-discharged for 60 s or 90 s at 20 mA or 15 mA using a PELCO easiGlow glow discharge system (Ted Pella). Approximately 1000–3000 cells were deposited onto a grid by pipetting 3 µL of detached cells onto the EM grid. Blotting and plunging was performed in a FEI Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc (TFS)) at RT, 100% humidity with a waiting time of 60 s, one-side blotting time of 15 s and blotting force of 10 or 7. Customized paraﬁlm sheets were used for one-sided blotting. All
